recipes.name: Monthly close & management pack
recipes.outcome: A completed close checklist, reconciliations with exceptions, and a one-page management pack.
recipes.when_to_use: Month-end is here (or overdue), the books are 'roughly right', and you want reconciled accounts, a clean close checklist and one page that tells you how the month really went, without losing your weekend to spreadsheets.

inputs_from_owner.label: Which month or period to close
inputs_from_owner.example: September 2026

inputs_from_owner.label: Accounting system, plus the bank, card and payment accounts to include
inputs_from_owner.example: QuickBooks Online; two bank accounts, one Amex, Stripe and Square payouts

inputs_from_owner.label: This year's budget or targets, if you have them
inputs_from_owner.example: Budget tab in the 2026 plan spreadsheet

inputs_from_owner.label: Anything unusual this month the books should know about
inputs_from_owner.example: Bought a van on finance; one big customer prepaid for Q4

inputs_from_owner.label: Does an outside accountant review your books, and how should we reach them?
inputs_from_owner.example: Our CPA firm reviews quarterly; email is fine

inputs_from_owner.label: The smallest difference worth chasing
inputs_from_owner.example: Anything over $50

composition.why: Thomas owns the close. He runs the checklist, proposes accruals and adjusting entries with support, and keeps accounting policy consistent from month to month.
Imelda categorizes every transaction, grows the rules library and reconciles bank, card and payout accounts to the penny.
Guillermo turns the closed numbers into a one-page management pack with a so-what an owner can read in two minutes.
Gulnara speaks for your future auditor or lender. She samples entries back to support, checks who approved what, and blocks the pack if the numbers don't tie.

plan_skeleton.title: Categorize the month's transactions
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Every bank, card and payout transaction in the period is coded to the chart of accounts with a memo, or listed as a question for the owner; receipt coverage % is reported; new rules are added to the rules library.
plan_skeleton.brief: Pull the period's feeds from the accounting connector (or uploaded statements), apply the existing rules and code the rest. Batch the questions only the owner can answer into one inbox card.

plan_skeleton.title: Reconcile bank, card and payout accounts
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Each account reconciles to its statement ending balance with zero unexplained difference, or every exception is listed with amount, age, cause and proposed fix; payout clearing accounts net to fees and refunds.
plan_skeleton.brief: Tie bank, credit card and Stripe/Square/PayPal clearing accounts to their statements, match deposits to payouts, and list uncleared items older than 30 days.

plan_skeleton.title: Run the close checklist and propose adjustments
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Checklist complete with a preparer and a reviewer for every step; accruals, prepaids, deferred revenue, depreciation and payroll entries proposed with support and rationale; nothing posted to the ledger without approval.
plan_skeleton.brief: Work the double-entry close checklist: cut-off, accruals, prepaids, deferrals, fixed assets, payroll liabilities and the sales-tax liability tie-out. Propose entries as a journal file for approval.

plan_skeleton.title: Controls spot-check
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES. At least ten entries traced to source documents; segregation-of-duties conflicts in this month's approvals and payments listed with a compensating control; formula errors in the close workbook flagged.
plan_skeleton.brief: Sample high-value and unusual entries, compare who approved each one with who created it, and audit the close workbook's formulas and links.

plan_skeleton.title: Licensed review of adjusting and tax-sensitive entries
plan_skeleton.acceptance: The owner's accountant (CPA, EA or chartered accountant) has reviewed the proposed entries and tax-sensitive items (sales tax, payroll liabilities, fixed-asset treatment). Their comments are recorded; approved entries are marked for posting and the rest are parked with a reason.
plan_skeleton.brief: Package the proposed entries with their support for the owner's accountant; filings, elections and tax positions stay with them. If no one reviews monthly, the owner decides which items wait for the next scheduled review.

plan_skeleton.title: Budget-versus-actual variance review
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Actuals compared with budget (or with last year, if there is no budget) by revenue line and expense group; every variance above the materiality threshold is explained by cause (price, volume, timing or one-off) with a source.
plan_skeleton.brief: Use the closed trial balance. Separate timing differences from real ones, and say which variances will reverse next month.

plan_skeleton.title: One-page management pack
plan_skeleton.acceptance: One page covering cash position and change, revenue, gross margin, operating expenses versus budget, the top three variances with cause and action, and open reconciliation exceptions. Every number ties to a cell in the close workbook, and items awaiting the accountant's review are marked.
plan_skeleton.brief: Pyramid Principle: lead with the answer (for example 'a solid month; margin down 2 points on freight'), then the three things that explain it, then what to do next.

deliverables.name: Close checklist with sign-offs
deliverables.description: Every close step with preparer, reviewer, date and evidence link.

deliverables.name: Reconciliation workbook and exceptions list
deliverables.description: One tab per account, tied to statements, with aged exceptions.

deliverables.name: Proposed adjusting entries with support
deliverables.description: Journal entries awaiting approval, each with rationale and a source document.

deliverables.name: Categorization rules library
deliverables.description: Reusable vendor and memo rules that cut next month's manual coding.

deliverables.name: One-page management pack
deliverables.description: The month in one page, with every number traceable to the close workbook.

deliverables.name: Two-minute month-in-review briefing
deliverables.description: The management pack, voiced by Guillermo.

meeting_moments.title: Close kickoff: cut-off and known surprises
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Thomas sets the cut-off date and the materiality line, Imelda reads out the handful of transactions only you can explain, and Gulnara says which controls she'll test this month. Five minutes, and you can answer Imelda's questions live.

meeting_moments.title: Exceptions critique
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Gulnara walks through the reconciliation exceptions and control findings while Imelda and Thomas propose fixes. You hear which items are timing noise, which need your decision and which go to your accountant.

meeting_moments.title: The month in two minutes
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Guillermo presents the management pack as a two-minute voiced briefing (the headline, three reasons and what to do), and Thomas adds anything still waiting on your accountant.

duration_estimate.note: Faster from the second month, once the rules library and checklist exist. The accountant's turnaround comes on top. In the year-end month, the full team adds Shira to turn the close into a clean organ

lines: Revenue 84.2k (plan 80k); gross margin 38.1% (down 1.4 points on freight).
All 5 accounts reconciled; 2 exceptions: a 312 duplicate supplier payment and a 1,040 deposit in transit.
Cash 41k, 6.2 weeks of costs; overdue receivables 23k.
Two actions: claim the duplicate refund and chase the three oldest invoices.

success_criteria: Every in-scope account is reconciled to its statement, or each exception is listed with amount, age and owner.
The close checklist shows a preparer and a reviewer for every step and is completed within the agreed number of business days.
Every number in the management pack ties to a cell in the close workbook.
The count of uncategorized transactions falls month over month as the rules library grows.
No entry is posted to the ledger without the owner's approval, and tax-sensitive items carry the accountant's comments.

variants_by_industry.changes: Adds tip-liability and gift-card tie-outs, daily POS-to-deposit matching and a weekly prime-cost line in the pack.
Adds a job-cost review and a work-in-progress schedule (over- and under-billings by job), retainage receivable and payable, and change orders not yet billed.
Reconciles Shopify, Amazon and marketplace payouts through clearing accounts (fees, refunds, reserves), books inventory and COGS from stock movements, and shows margin by channel.
Adds a deferred-revenue roll-forward, revenue-recognition checks for annual plans and an MRR-to-revenue reconciliation in the pack.
Tracks restricted and unrestricted funds, grant spending against each award budget and in-kind gifts; the pack reports by program and funding source.
Job costing by job type and a work-in-progress list for multi-visit jobs; customer deposits tracked as liabilities until the work is done.

recipes.name: Cash runway rescue
recipes.outcome: A 13-week cash forecast, runway view and a ranked list of cash levers with owners.
recipes.when_to_use: Cash is tighter than it should be. Payroll feels close, customers are paying late, or you simply don't know how many weeks you have. You want a week-by-week view and the moves that buy the most time, fast.

inputs_from_owner.label: Current cash across all accounts (or connect your bank or accounting feed)
inputs_from_owner.example: $84k across operating and savings; $20k undrawn credit line

inputs_from_owner.label: Who owes you and whom you owe (aging reports or a list)
inputs_from_owner.example: AR and AP aging exported from Xero

inputs_from_owner.label: Payroll dates and amounts, rent, loans and other fixed commitments
inputs_from_owner.example: Biweekly payroll about $31k; rent $6.5k on the 1st; loan $2.1k on the 15th

inputs_from_owner.label: Big receipts or payments expected in the next 13 weeks
inputs_from_owner.example: $40k customer milestone mid-November; quarterly tax payment in January

inputs_from_owner.label: The lowest cash balance you're comfortable with
inputs_from_owner.example: Never below one payroll

inputs_from_owner.label: Levers that are off the table
inputs_from_owner.example: No layoffs; don't touch the marketing retainer

composition.why: Harriet builds the 13-week cash forecast and the runway view, ranks the levers, and explains financing options as mechanics, never as advice.
Andre pulls cash forward from receivables with a polite, firm dunning ladder and payment-plan offers that keep customers.
Tendai finds the cost and margin levers (what to cut, defer or reprice) and shows what each does to break-even.
Idris plans the supplier, landlord and lender conversations with a BATNA and a concession sequence, and chairs the lever decision.
Putri speaks for the week the forecast gets wrong. She stress-tests receipts with seasonality and late payers and puts an honest range on the runway.

plan_skeleton.title: Build the 13-week cash forecast
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Weekly receipts and disbursements for 13 weeks from the actual opening balance; every line has a driver and a source; the lowest-cash week and the date cash falls below the owner's buffer are flagged; base and downside cases included.
plan_skeleton.brief: Use the direct method. Time collections from the AR aging and payments from AP and fixed commitments, and include the payroll calendar, debt service and tax dates.

plan_skeleton.title: Receivables pull-forward plan
plan_skeleton.acceptance: AR aging with DSO; accounts ranked by amount times days overdue; a dunning ladder and payment-plan offers drafted for each bucket; expected cash pulled forward shown by week; nothing is sent without the owner's approval.
plan_skeleton.brief: Protect relationships: start with a friendly reminder, escalate by bucket, and offer a payment plan before any firm language.

plan_skeleton.title: Cost and margin levers
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Costs split into fixed and variable; each of the top 15 spend lines has a cut, defer or renegotiate option with its cash effect by week and its operational risk; break-even revenue recalculated.
plan_skeleton.brief: Start from the last three months of actuals. Flag subscriptions, duplicate tools and discretionary spend first, and price-sensitive margin fixes second.

plan_skeleton.title: Stress-test the forecast
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES. Receipts re-estimated with seasonality and an 80% interval; a downside case where the three largest customers pay 30 days late; runway stated as a range, not a single date.
plan_skeleton.brief: Backtest the receipts assumptions against the last six months of actual collections before challenging them.

plan_skeleton.title: Supplier, landlord and lender talk tracks
plan_skeleton.acceptance: For each counterparty worth calling: the ask, the BATNA, the likely zone of agreement, a concession sequence and a short script, plus the weeks of runway each ask could buy. The team contacts no counterparty.
plan_skeleton.brief: Prioritize counterparties by cash at stake and relationship strength. The owner makes the calls; the scripts are written for them.

plan_skeleton.title: Ranked cash levers and runway view
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Levers ranked by cash gained, speed and risk, each with an owner, a first action and the week it lands; runway shown before and after; financing options explained as mechanics only, with no recommendation to borrow or raise.
plan_skeleton.brief: One page plus the model. Say plainly which levers the owner can pull this week without anyone else's permission.

plan_skeleton.title: Licensed review of financing and tax levers
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Any lever involving new debt or equity, loan covenants, or delayed tax or payroll-tax payments has been reviewed by the owner's accountant or a licensed financial adviser before any action. Their comments are recorded against each lever.
plan_skeleton.brief: Harriet is not a licensed adviser and says so. Operational levers (collections, cost cuts) can proceed on the owner's approval alone.

deliverables.name: 13-week cash forecast (base and downside)
deliverables.description: Direct-method forecast with drivers, sources and a lowest-cash-week flag.

deliverables.name: Ranked cash levers with owners and dates
Collection emails and payment-plan offers
deliverables.description: Drafts only; nothing is sent without approval.

deliverables.name: Weekly cash briefing
deliverables.description: Two minutes each week: cash today, the low point and which levers have landed.

meeting_moments.title: Cash kickoff: how many weeks do we really have?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Harriet shares a first rough runway number and the assumptions behind it, Andre names the invoices most likely to move, and Putri says which assumption she trusts least. You can correct anything they've got wrong about your business.

meeting_moments.title: Is the runway real?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Putri argues the downside (late payers, a soft month) and Harriet defends the base case. Idris keeps both to the evidence and closes with a range everyone accepts, so you know exactly how confident to be.

meeting_moments.title: Which levers do we pull this week?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Idris chairs. Each coworker pitches their top lever in one sentence, with cash gained, speed and risk. You choose. Anything that touches financing or tax goes to your accountant or adviser first.

duration_estimate.note: First forecast within a day, then a weekly refresh of about 30 minutes until the runway is safe.

lines: Lowest cash week: week 7 at -8.4k in the base case, -19k in the downside.
Top levers: collect 3 overdue invoices (+21k by week 4) and move the equipment payment to week 9 (+6k).
Supplier talk track ready for the two largest creditors.
Mechanics only: financing options are explained, not recommended; a licensed adviser reviews any borrowing.

success_criteria: The forecast starts from the actual bank balance, and every line names its driver and source.
The lowest-cash week is identified, and the runway is stated as a range rather than a single date.
At least five levers are ranked, each with an owner, a first action and the week its cash lands.
At week four, forecast cash is within 10% of actual, or the gap is explained.
No money moves and no counterparty is contacted without the owner's approval, and financing and tax levers get professional review first.

variants_by_industry.changes: Adds burn multiple, MRR-driven receipts, annual-prepay and collections levers, and months of runway at current burn.
Adds cash tied up in inventory: slow movers to clear, reorder timing and supplier payment terms become levers.
Adds progress-billing and retainage timing, unbilled change orders and job-level cash curves.
Adds weekly prime cost, seasonal covers, gift-card float and supplier COD terms as levers.
Separates restricted from unrestricted cash, and adds grant disbursement timing and a donor appeal as receipt levers.
Seasonal cash: deposits, membership prepayments and a slow-season buffer; open quotes are chased before any cost is cut.

recipes.name: Annual plan, OKRs & budget
recipes.outcome: A strategy one-pager, quarterly OKRs and a driver-based annual budget.
recipes.when_to_use: A new year (or fiscal year) is coming and you want more than a revenue guess: a few clear choices, quarterly goals the team can own, and a budget built from drivers you can actually steer.

inputs_from_owner.label: The last 12 months of financials (connect accounting or upload)
inputs_from_owner.example: P&L and balance sheet from QuickBooks

inputs_from_owner.label: What a great year looks like to you
inputs_from_owner.example: Grow revenue 25% without working weekends; open a second location by Q3

inputs_from_owner.label: When your fiscal year starts
inputs_from_owner.example: January

inputs_from_owner.label: Things that won't change
inputs_from_owner.example: Keep prices below the big chain; no new debt

inputs_from_owner.label: People you plan to hire, lose or move
inputs_from_owner.example: Hire a second technician in Q2

inputs_from_owner.label: Any existing plan, strategy document or goals
inputs_from_owner.example: Last year's goals in Notion

composition.why: Adaeze forces the real choices (where to play, how to win and what to stop) onto one page, grounded in last year's evidence.
Ingrid turns the choices into quarterly OKRs with owners, baselines and a check-in rhythm people actually keep.
Farah builds the driver-based budget and ties every target back to the plan.
Elijah designs and runs the planning workshop you join, with timeboxes and a clear decision rule.
Kenji speaks for the year that doesn't go to plan. He brings scenarios with signposts and a downside the budget must survive.

plan_skeleton.title: Last-year review and run-rate baseline
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Twelve months of actuals versus plan (or versus the prior year) by revenue line and cost group; the top five variances explained; a run-rate baseline for next year with one-offs removed.
plan_skeleton.brief: Normalize for one-offs and seasonality so next year's baseline reflects how the business actually runs.

plan_skeleton.title: Strategy choices one-pager
plan_skeleton.acceptance: One page covering winning aspiration, where to play, how to win, required capabilities and management systems; three things the business will stop doing; every choice tied to evidence from the review.
plan_skeleton.brief: Draft the Playing to Win cascade from the owner's ambition and last year's evidence. Present at most three candidate choices for the workshop to decide.

plan_skeleton.title: Scenarios and signposts
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Two or three plausible scenarios, each with the early-warning signposts to watch, the revenue and cost sensitivities the budget must test, and the no-regret moves.
plan_skeleton.brief: Keep the scenarios specific to this business and its market; skip generic macro stories.

plan_skeleton.title: Planning workshop
plan_skeleton.acceptance: An owner-joined session with a timeboxed agenda and a stated decision rule; choices confirmed or changed and recorded; the top three priorities for the year agreed; parked items listed.
plan_skeleton.brief: Use 1-2-4-All on the candidate choices, then consent-based decisions. Kenji plays each scenario against the choices before they are locked.

plan_skeleton.title: Quarterly OKRs
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Next-quarter OKRs with at most three objectives and two to four measurable key results each, plus baselines, owners and a confidence score; intent for the remaining quarters; every key result traced to a strategic choice.
plan_skeleton.brief: Key results measure outcomes, not tasks. Add the weekly check-in question each owner will answer.

plan_skeleton.title: Driver-based annual budget
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A monthly P&L and cash budget built from documented drivers (volume × price, headcount × loaded cost, % of revenue); totals tie to the OKR targets; a downside tab built from Kenji's scenarios shows whether cash stays above the owner's buffer and flags the month it doesn't.
plan_skeleton.brief: Every assumption lives on one drivers tab, so the owner can change a driver and watch the budget move.

deliverables.name: Quarterly OKRs with owners and baselines
Driver-based annual budget with a downside tab
Budget bridge from run-rate to plan

meeting_moments.title: What does a great year look like?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Elijah interviews you for twenty minutes about your ambition, what you'd never trade and what last year taught you. Adaeze listens for the real choices, Ingrid for measurable goals, and Farah for the numbers behind them.

meeting_moments.title: Strategy choices workshop
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Elijah runs a 1-2-4-All on the draft choices, Kenji plays each scenario against them, and you decide by consent. You leave with three priorities and a written stop-doing list.

meeting_moments.title: Does the budget survive a bad year?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Kenji argues the downside, Farah defends the drivers, and Adaeze says which choice she would protect first. Elijah closes with the one change that makes the plan robust.

meeting_moments.title: Approve the plan
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: A five-minute DACI decision: Adaeze presents the one-pager, Ingrid the Q1 OKRs and Farah the budget. You approve, or name the one thing to change.

duration_estimate.note: Two working sessions with you, about 90 minutes in total. Everything else runs in the background.

lines: Where to play: repeat commercial clients within 30 miles; stop chasing one-off residential jobs.
How to win: guaranteed response times with a named technician.
Q1 objective: become the default for 20 commercial accounts. KR: 12 signed service agreements (baseline 4).
Budget: revenue +14% with 2 hires timed for the April peak; downside tab holds hiring until Q2.

success_criteria: The strategy fits on one page and names at least three things the business will stop doing.
Every key result is measurable, has a baseline and an owner, and traces to a strategic choice.
Every budget line comes from a documented driver, and the totals match the OKR targets.
The downside scenario has been run, and the plan shows the cash low point against the owner's buffer.
The owner's approval of the plan is recorded as a decision.

variants_by_industry.changes: Budgets by program and funding source (restricted and unrestricted), with a theory-of-change link from each program to its outcome key results.
Adds ARR, NRR and burn-multiple drivers, a hiring plan by quarter and a board-ready summary.
Drivers become billable headcount, utilization, realization and the rate card; OKRs include pipeline coverage.
Capacity and OEE constraints feed the volume drivers, and capex and maintenance windows go into the budget.
Seasonal covers and average check drive revenue; prime-cost targets and a labor model anchor costs.

recipes.name: Business plan for a lender or partner
recipes.outcome: A lender- or partner-ready business plan with financial projections and risks.
recipes.when_to_use: You're applying for a bank loan, a government-backed small-business loan, equipment finance or a partnership, and they want a business plan with projections that shows exactly how the money comes back.

inputs_from_owner.label: Who the plan is for and what you're asking for
inputs_from_owner.example: Community bank; $250k term loan for a second kitchen

inputs_from_owner.label: Two to three years of financial statements (or connect accounting)
inputs_from_owner.example: 2023–2025 P&Ls and balance sheets

inputs_from_owner.label: How the money will be used, and when
inputs_from_owner.example: $180k equipment, $50k build-out, $20k working capital

inputs_from_owner.label: The lender's or partner's template or checklist, if any
inputs_from_owner.example: The bank's loan application checklist (PDF)

inputs_from_owner.label: Key people and their experience
inputs_from_owner.example: Owner (12 years in catering), head chef, part-time bookkeeper

inputs_from_owner.label: Existing loans and leases, and any collateral you could offer
inputs_from_owner.example: Van loan with $18k remaining; equipment as collateral

composition.why: Harriet builds the linked three-statement projections with debt service, and keeps every number defensible in front of a credit officer.
Tomás owns the business narrative: the model, what the money unlocks and why the plan is credible.
Arturo brings the bottom-up market sizing and competitor evidence lenders look for, with every source cited.
Theodora makes the plan read as if one confident author wrote it, handling the structure, the executive summary and the final polish.
Ruth plays the credit officer who isn't in the room. She lists the ten questions they'll ask and builds a downside case that still has to repay.

plan_skeleton.title: Business model and use of funds
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A Business Model Canvas backed by the owner's facts, stating exactly what the funds buy, when, and which revenue or cost line each purchase changes.
plan_skeleton.brief: Start from what the lender is really underwriting: the cash flow the new money creates.

plan_skeleton.title: Market and competitor evidence
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A bottom-up serviceable market with cited sources and stated assumptions; target segments with evidence; named direct or local competitors and how the business differs.
plan_skeleton.brief: Lenders discount top-down TAM claims. Build from customers, locations and price points.

plan_skeleton.title: Three-statement projections with debt service
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Linked P&L, balance sheet and cash flow, monthly for year one and annual for years two and three (or the lender's horizon); loan drawdown and repayment modeled; debt-service coverage ratio computed; an assumptions tab with a source for every driver; the balance sheet balances in every period.
plan_skeleton.brief: Anchor the projections in historical actuals and show the bridge from last year to year one.

plan_skeleton.title: Business plan draft
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Executive summary, company, market, operations, management, financials, use of funds, and risks with mitigations; every figure matches the model; the sections follow the stated lender's checklist.
plan_skeleton.brief: Write for a credit officer with twenty minutes: clear headings, numbers in tables and no hype.

plan_skeleton.title: Credit officer red-team
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES. The ten questions a credit officer will ask, each with the plan's answer or a named gap; a downside with revenue 20% below plan that still shows repayment, or states the shortfall plainly.
plan_skeleton.brief: Speak for the lender: repayment capacity, collateral, the owner's experience and what happens if the key person is unavailable.

plan_skeleton.title: Executive summary and final edit
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A one-page executive summary that states the ask, the use of funds and how the loan is repaid; consistent terms and numbers throughout; every gap Ruth raised is answered or disclosed.
plan_skeleton.brief: Structural edit first, then line edit. Never change a number without checking the model.

plan_skeleton.title: Licensed review before submission
plan_skeleton.acceptance: The owner's accountant or a licensed financial adviser has reviewed the projections and the financing terms. Their comments are resolved or listed, and the owner approves before anything goes to the lender.
plan_skeleton.brief: The team explains mechanics and models the owner's own scenarios. Whether to take this loan is the owner's decision, made with their licensed adviser.

deliverables.name: Three-statement projection model
deliverables.description: Linked statements with debt service, a DSCR and an assumptions tab.

deliverables.name: Credit officer Q&A prep
deliverables.description: The ten hardest questions and the answers the plan supports.

deliverables.name: Revenue, cash and debt-service coverage charts

meeting_moments.title: What's the ask, and who says yes?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Harriet asks what you need and how you'll repay it, Tomás asks what the money unlocks, and Arturo asks who your customers and competitors really are. Fifteen minutes that save a week of guessing.

meeting_moments.title: Mock credit committee
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Ruth plays the credit officer and grills the plan while Harriet and Tomás answer. You hear the hardest questions in a safe room, and which answers still need work before the real meeting.

meeting_moments.title: Your plan in three minutes
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Theodora reads the executive summary aloud, and Harriet walks through the three numbers a lender looks at first: debt-service coverage, the cash low point and collateral cover. It doubles as a rehearsal for your own pitch.

duration_estimate.note: Includes one 15-minute interview. The accountant's or adviser's review time comes on top.

lines: Use of funds: 85k for a second van and equipment, tied to 2 commercial contracts already signed.
Debt-service coverage 1.6x in the base case and 1.25x in the downside.
Likely question: what if the largest client leaves? Answer: it is 18% of revenue; plan B is shown.
The plan is for your lender and accountant to review; no guarantee terms are suggested.

success_criteria: The model is fully linked: the balance sheet balances in every period and cash ties to the cash-flow statement.
Debt-service coverage is shown by year, with a downside case.
Every market claim cites a source, and every figure in the plan matches the model.
Every item on the lender's checklist is answered or listed as a known gap.
The accountant or adviser has reviewed the plan and the owner has approved it before submission.

variants_by_industry.changes: A new-location plan: site and catchment evidence, a build-out budget, a covers ramp-up curve and prime-cost targets.
Leads with backlog, bonding capacity, equipment finance and job-margin history.
An equipment loan where capacity, OEE improvement and the payback of the new line drive the projections.
Revenue-based financing or venture debt: MRR cohorts, churn and burn multiple drive the model.
A partner or program-related-investment plan with a logic model, outcomes and a sources-and-uses budget.

recipes.name: Hire for a role
recipes.outcome: A job description, sourcing plan, structured interview kit and an offer-letter draft for review.
recipes.when_to_use: You need to hire and want to get it right first time: a clear role, a fair pay range, a structured process that picks the best person rather than the best talker, and an offer ready for review.

inputs_from_owner.label: The role, why you need it now and what success looks like in year one
inputs_from_owner.example: Operations coordinator. I'm drowning in scheduling and supplier calls

inputs_from_owner.label: The pay budget or range you have in mind
inputs_from_owner.example: $55–65k plus benefits

inputs_from_owner.label: Location and work arrangement (on-site, hybrid or remote; which states or countries)
inputs_from_owner.example: Hybrid, Austin TX

inputs_from_owner.label: Target start date
inputs_from_owner.example: Early January

inputs_from_owner.label: Who will interview
inputs_from_owner.example: Me and our lead technician

inputs_from_owner.label: Current pay for similar roles, used only for the internal equity check and kept confidential
inputs_from_owner.example: Two coordinators at $52k and $58k

composition.why: Leila runs structured hiring end to end: scorecard, job description, sourcing, interview kit and the offer draft.

plan_skeleton.title: Role scorecard and job description
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A scorecard with the mission, three to five measurable year-one outcomes and the competencies (Who method); a job description built from it that separates must-haves from nice-to-haves, uses inclusive language and has a slot for the pay range.
plan_skeleton.brief: Write the outcomes before the requirements; every must-have has to earn its place against an outcome.

plan_skeleton.title: Market pay range and internal equity check
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A market range from at least three cited sources for this role, level and location; a proposed band with midpoint; the internal equity check against current pay shown to the owner only; pay-transparency posting rules noted by location.
plan_skeleton.brief: Benchmark the scorecard, not the job title. Current employees' pay data stays confidential and minimized.

plan_skeleton.title: Sourcing plan and outreach
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Channels ranked for this role, Boolean search strings, two outreach templates, a plan for a diverse candidate slate and a weekly funnel target, using only information candidates have published professionally.
plan_skeleton.brief: Include referral and community channels as well as job boards. Outreach templates are drafts, sent only on the owner's approval.

plan_skeleton.title: Structured interview kit
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Stage plan; structured questions mapped to every competency; a behaviourally anchored 1–4 rating scale; one realistic work sample; interviewer assignments; a debrief protocol in which everyone scores before discussion.
plan_skeleton.brief: Same questions for every candidate, in the same order. Work samples are paid or kept under two hours.

plan_skeleton.title: Offer letter draft
plan_skeleton.acceptance: An offer letter draft with role, start date, pay, benefits summary, contingencies and employment-terms language flagged by jurisdiction; placeholders for anything unknown; clearly marked DRAFT for review.
plan_skeleton.brief: Use the owner's template if one exists. Every legally sensitive clause carries a jurisdiction flag.

plan_skeleton.title: Licensed review of posting and offer
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Employment counsel or a qualified HR professional has reviewed classification, the pay-transparency posting and the offer template, and a privacy professional or counsel has cleared the candidate-data handling. Changes are applied, and nothing is posted or sent before the owner approves.
plan_skeleton.brief: Desmond packages the posting, the band and the offer draft with his flags; Sebastián prepares the privacy part (search methods, candidate data kept and for how long). Record each of counsel's decisions.

deliverables.name: Structured interview kit and rating sheet
Offer letter draft for review
deliverables.description: Marked DRAFT; jurisdiction flags on sensitive clauses.

meeting_moments.title: Hiring-manager intake

meeting_moments.title: Would this kit pick the right person?

meeting_moments.title: What you're approving

lines: Mission: make every job run on time without the owner chasing suppliers.

plan_skeleton.title: New-hire journey map

plan_skeleton.title: Joiner and leaver access SOP

plan_skeleton.title: Manager and buddy guide

plan_skeleton.title: Day-one walkthrough test
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES. A simulated new hire walks through day one and week one against the plan; every confusing step, missing access, broken link or unowned task is logged with a fix.

meeting_moments.title: Day-one walkthrough

recipes.name: Handbook & core policies

composition.why: Desmond drafts the handbook and policies in plain language, with a jurisdiction flag on every legally sensitive clause, ready for employment counsel.
Manuel knows how policies land with managers and staff. He owns the gap review and the core policy drafts.
Suresh makes it readable and rolls it out: the plain-language pass, employee FAQ, manager talking points and acknowledgement tracking.
Remy checks the policies for inclusive language, accessible formats and a clear accommodation route.
Anneke speaks for the regulator in each location. She checks every policy against primary-source requirements and names what's missing or out of date.
Sebastián reviews the employee-data, monitoring and retention policies so the handbook collects only what the business needs.

plan_skeleton.title: Jurisdiction requirements matrix
plan_skeleton.acceptance: For each location where people work: required policies, notices, posters and leave entitlements from primary sources, with citations and last-checked dates; unknowns and pending law changes flagged.
plan_skeleton.brief: Use official government and regulator sources first; secondary summaries only to find them.

plan_skeleton.title: Current policy gap review
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Current documents mapped against a core list (conduct, anti-harassment and complaints, leave, time and pay, remote work, IT and AI use, privacy, safety, accommodations), each marked keep, update, new or retire with the reason.
plan_skeleton.brief: Note where current practice differs from what is written, because those gaps cause the most disputes.

plan_skeleton.title: Handbook draft
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Handbook sections in plain language with a jurisdiction flag on every legally sensitive clause; no clause claims to be legally compliant; an acknowledgement form included.
plan_skeleton.brief: Where locations differ, use a clear base policy with location-specific supplements, not buried exceptions.

plan_skeleton.title: Core standalone policies
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Standalone drafts for the anti-harassment and complaint procedure, leave, remote and hybrid work, and acceptable use (including AI tools), each with scope, owner, procedure, jurisdiction flags and a review date.
plan_skeleton.brief: The acceptable-use policy says which AI tools may see customer or employee data and which may not.

plan_skeleton.title: Plain-language pass and employee FAQ
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Reading level at or below grade 8 wherever the legal meaning allows; any wording change that could alter legal meaning is flagged for Desmond; an FAQ answering the 15 questions employees will ask first.
plan_skeleton.brief: Test the FAQ against real questions from the owner's inbox or chat history.

plan_skeleton.title: Licensed review by employment counsel
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Employment counsel has reviewed the flagged clauses and the jurisdiction matrix; every comment is resolved or logged; the owner approves the final text before distribution.
plan_skeleton.brief: Send counsel a packet with the drafts, the flags and the matrix, not a blank request to review everything.

plan_skeleton.title: Rollout and acknowledgement plan
plan_skeleton.acceptance: An announcement, manager talking points, a Q&A session plan and acknowledgement tracking; nothing is distributed until the owner approves.
plan_skeleton.brief: Managers hear it first, with answers to the three questions they'll get most.

recipes.name: Contract review desk
recipes.outcome: An issue list with suggested redlines and a negotiation note, packaged for attorney review.
recipes.when_to_use: A contract has landed (a supplier agreement, lease, customer MSA or partnership) and you need to know what you're agreeing to, what to push back on and how, before you or your attorney sign anything.

inputs_from_owner.label: The contract, its exhibits and any prior versions
inputs_from_owner.example: Vendor MSA, order form and DPA (PDF)

inputs_from_owner.label: Which side you're on and what the deal is
inputs_from_owner.example: We're the customer, buying a 3-year software licence

inputs_from_owner.label: What matters most: price, speed, flexibility or risk
inputs_from_owner.example: Need it live by March; can't accept auto-renewal over 1 year

inputs_from_owner.label: Your standard positions or past contracts, if any
inputs_from_owner.example: Our last two vendor contracts

inputs_from_owner.label: Your relationship with the other side and your leverage
inputs_from_owner.example: They want our logo as a reference; two competitors are close

inputs_from_owner.label: Your attorney and how to reach them
inputs_from_owner.example: Outside counsel, by email

composition.why: Eleanor reviews every clause against a playbook and writes the issue list, with plain-English risk, suggested redlines and fallbacks for your attorney.
Ezra triages the documents, extracts key terms and dates, and files the approved positions in your clause library for next time.
Sebastián checks the data-processing, security and confidentiality terms against a DPA checklist.
Idris turns the issue list into a negotiation plan (must-haves, tradeables, BATNA) and chairs the sign, negotiate or walk debate.
Viktor speaks for the team that will live with this contract. He lists every obligation, SLA, penalty and renewal, with what it costs and the worst case.

plan_skeleton.title: Document intake and key terms
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Contract, exhibits and prior versions parsed; parties, term, value, governing law, renewal and notice dates, and termination rights extracted to a key-terms sheet; missing exhibits or referenced documents flagged.
plan_skeleton.brief: Compare against prior versions if supplied and list every change.

plan_skeleton.title: Issue list with suggested redlines
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Every clause compared with the owner's playbook (or a stated default position); issues ranked high, medium or low with plain-English risk, a suggested redline and a fallback; jurisdiction assumptions stated; nothing presented as legal advice.
plan_skeleton.brief: Lead with the five issues that matter most. Low-risk boilerplate gets one line, not a paragraph.

plan_skeleton.title: Data and security terms check
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Data-processing, security, confidentiality and breach-notice terms checked against a DPA checklist; gaps listed with suggested clauses; marked not applicable, with the reason, if no personal data flows.
plan_skeleton.brief: Check the sub-processor list and the transfer mechanism, not just the DPA's existence.

plan_skeleton.title: Obligations and exposure check
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES. Every obligation, SLA, penalty, price escalator and auto-renewal the business must live with is listed with who performs it, what it costs and the worst-case exposure; any issue the list under-rates is escalated.
plan_skeleton.brief: Read the contract as the person who has to perform it on a bad day.

plan_skeleton.title: Negotiation note
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Must-haves, tradeables and walk-aways; the BATNA and likely zone of agreement; a concession sequence and email-ready talking points. No message is sent to the counterparty.
plan_skeleton.brief: Trade what is cheap for us and valuable to them. Name the one ask worth walking away over.

plan_skeleton.title: Licensed review: attorney packet and decisions
plan_skeleton.acceptance: The attorney packet (key terms, issue list, redlines, data-terms gaps and open questions) is delivered; the attorney's decision on each issue is recorded; nothing is signed or sent before this review and the owner's approval.
plan_skeleton.brief: Eleanor is not an attorney and says so. The packet saves the attorney time; it doesn't replace their judgement.

plan_skeleton.title: Clause library and obligations tracker
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Attorney-approved positions and fallbacks are saved to the clause library with source and date; renewal, notice and obligation dates are added to a tracker, with reminders proposed for owner approval.
plan_skeleton.brief: Record only positions the attorney approved, marked with the matter and date.

deliverables.name: Issue list with suggested redlines
deliverables.description: Ranked issues with plain-English risk, redline and fallback, for attorney review.

meeting_moments.title: What does this contract commit us to?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Ezra reads out the key terms in plain English (term, price, renewal, how to get out), and Eleanor names the three clauses she's worried about before the full review. Viktor asks who on your team will actually do what the contract promises.

meeting_moments.title: Sign, negotiate or walk?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Idris chairs. Eleanor argues the legal risks, Viktor the operational ones and Sebastián the data terms. It ends with a ranked ask list and a walk-away line for you to take to your attorney.

meeting_moments.title: Your attorney packet
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Eleanor summarises the packet going to your attorney and the decisions they need to make, and Idris gives the negotiation plan in two minutes.

duration_estimate.note: The attorney's turnaround comes on top.

lines: High: unlimited liability for data breaches (clause 9.2): propose a cap at 12 months of fees.

Medium: exclusivity in your region (clause 5.1): ask for a carve-out.
Packaged for your attorney; nothing here is legal advice.

success_criteria: Every clause is either marked acceptable or listed with a risk rating, a suggested redline and a fallback.
Every renewal, notice and termination date is captured in the obligations tracker.
The negotiation note states a walk-away position and a concession sequence.
An attorney has reviewed the packet, and nothing is signed or sent before the review and the owner's approval.
The approved positions are in the clause library, ready for the next contract.

Client SOWs and MSAs: scope, acceptance, IP ownership and change control.
Brand deals: usage rights, exclusivity, approval rounds, payment terms and sponsorship-disclosure clauses.
The firm's own vendor, engagement-letter and outside-counsel terms, with conflict and confidentiality checks.

recipes.name: Privacy & compliance baseline
recipes.outcome: A data map, privacy notice draft, vendor DPA check and compliance calendar for review.

inputs_from_owner.label: Tools that hold customer or staff data (or let us read enabled connectors)
inputs_from_owner.example: Shopify, Klaviyo, HubSpot, Gusto, Google Workspace, Zendesk

inputs_from_owner.label: What you collect and where (forms, checkout, CRM, cookies)
inputs_from_owner.example: Checkout, newsletter signup, contact form, Meta pixel

inputs_from_owner.label: Whether you use ad pixels, sell or share data, or use AI tools on customer data
inputs_from_owner.example: Meta and Google pixels; ChatGPT for support drafts

inputs_from_owner.label: Your current privacy notice (URL or file)
inputs_from_owner.example: example.com/privacy

inputs_from_owner.label: The privacy counsel or adviser who will review

composition.why: Sebastián builds the records of processing, the privacy notice draft and the vendor DPA check, stating his jurisdiction assumptions.
Amina turns obligations into a compliance calendar with owners and dates: reviews, renewals, request deadlines and training.
Luz traces how personal data really moves between your SaaS tools and connectors, and draws the flow.
Aoife makes the notice readable, with a layered plain-language summary people actually finish.

plan_skeleton.title: Personal data flow discovery
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Every system that stores or moves personal data (drawn from enabled connectors, invoices and the owner's list), with data categories, data subjects, hosting region and integrations, shown in a data-flow diagram.
plan_skeleton.brief: Read connector metadata and admin settings only. Never export or copy the personal data itself.

plan_skeleton.title: AI tools and tracking sweep
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES. AI tools, ad pixels, session recorders and data brokers in the stack listed with the personal data each receives and the vendor's terms on training and retention; anything missing from the data map is added.
plan_skeleton.brief: Check the website's tags, the helpdesk's AI features and staff use of general-purpose AI tools.

plan_skeleton.title: Records of processing (ROPA)
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Records of processing for each activity: purpose, assumed lawful basis, data categories, recipients, transfers, retention and safeguards; the GDPR, CCPA/CPRA or other regime assumed for each market is stated.
plan_skeleton.brief: Mark every lawful-basis entry as an assumption for counsel to confirm.

plan_skeleton.title: Vendor DPA check
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Each processor checked for a DPA, sub-processor list, transfer mechanism and security terms; gaps ranked by risk, with the vendor's standard DPA linked where available; no vendor is contacted without approval.
plan_skeleton.brief: Many vendors publish a click-through DPA; say whether it has been accepted.

plan_skeleton.title: Privacy notice draft
plan_skeleton.acceptance: The notice matches the records of processing exactly (nothing disclosed that isn't mapped, nothing mapped that isn't disclosed); rights and contact routes by market; a layered plain-language summary; marked as a draft for counsel.
plan_skeleton.brief: Write the layered summary first, then the full notice.

plan_skeleton.title: Compliance calendar
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Recurring obligations (notice review, DPA renewals, data-subject request deadlines, retention purges, staff training and a breach drill), each with an owner and a date; reminders are created only after owner approval.
plan_skeleton.brief: Keep it to obligations the business can actually run; flag anything that needs outside help.

plan_skeleton.title: Licensed review by privacy counsel
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A privacy professional or counsel has reviewed the records of processing, the notice and the DPA gaps; comments are resolved or logged; nothing is published or sent to vendors before the owner approves.
plan_skeleton.brief: Package the ROPA, the notice and the gap register with the jurisdiction assumptions clearly marked.

deliverables.name: Privacy notice draft with plain-language summary

meeting_moments.title: Where does customer data go?

meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Avery walks through each unexpected data flow (a pixel on the checkout, a support tool that trains on transcripts) and Sebastián rates the risk. You hear what to switch off now and what to disclose.

meeting_moments.title: Your privacy baseline in three minutes
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Sebastián summarises the map and the gaps, Amina reads out the next three dates on the calendar, and Aoife reads the notice's plain-language summary as a customer will see it.

duration_estimate.note: Counsel's review time comes on top.

Gaps: no DPA on file for 3 vendors; the booking form collects date of birth without a need.
Privacy notice draft and ROPA ready for counsel review.

success_criteria: Every system holding personal data appears on the data map and in the ROPA.
The notice and the ROPA match line by line.
Every processor has a DPA status, and every gap has a proposed fix.
Every recurring obligation has an owner and a date on the calendar.
Counsel has reviewed the ROPA and the notice, and nothing is published or sent without the owner's approval.

variants_by_industry.changes: A HIPAA lens: protected health information flows, Business Associate Agreements alongside DPAs, and minimum-necessary messaging.
Consent banners, pixel and conversion-API settings, marketing consent at checkout, and sale or share opt-outs where required.
You are a processor too: a customer-facing DPA, a sub-processor page and security answers that match the ROPA.
Flags for minors' and student data (such as COPPA- or FERPA-style rules where relevant) and parental consent flows.
Client confidentiality, conflicts data and privilege considerations layered onto the privacy map.

recipes.name: SOP & process library
recipes.outcome: Mapped core processes, improved SOPs and a searchable process library.
recipes.when_to_use: Too much of the business lives in people's heads. Training takes forever, quality depends on who's working, and you can't take a week off. You want the core processes mapped, improved and written down where everyone can find them.

inputs_from_owner.label: The processes that hurt or matter most
inputs_from_owner.example: Quoting, job scheduling, invoicing, new-customer setup

inputs_from_owner.label: Who does each process today
inputs_from_owner.example: Ana does quotes, Ben schedules, I invoice

inputs_from_owner.label: Where the library should live
inputs_from_owner.example: Notion

inputs_from_owner.label: Existing checklists, docs or training material
inputs_from_owner.example: Some Google Docs and a laminated opening checklist

inputs_from_owner.label: Tools used in these processes
inputs_from_owner.example: Jobber, QuickBooks, Gmail

composition.why: Lars maps the processes with SIPOC and swimlanes, removes waste with Lean before anything is written down, and runs the process walk.
Morgan writes SOPs people actually follow: numbered steps, the reason behind critical steps, visuals and a revision date.
Frankie builds the searchable library: structure, naming, owners, review dates and a glossary.
Felipe spots the manual steps worth automating later and sizes the hours they would save.
Dawit speaks for the new hire on a busy Friday. He cold-reads every SOP and asks whether anyone could follow it without asking.

plan_skeleton.title: Process inventory and priorities
plan_skeleton.acceptance: An inventory of core processes (for example order-to-cash, procure-to-pay, hire-to-retire and service delivery) with owner, frequency, pain and risk; the top eight chosen by frequency × risk × pain and agreed with the owner.
plan_skeleton.brief: Start from the owner's list, then add the processes that connectors and the calendar show happen every week.

plan_skeleton.title: Map the top processes
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A SIPOC and a swimlane map for each chosen process, with waits, hand-offs and rework marked; one improvement per process agreed with the person who does the work.
plan_skeleton.brief: Map the process as it runs today, then the improved version. Never write down waste as the standard.

plan_skeleton.title: SOP drafts
plan_skeleton.acceptance: One SOP per process, covering purpose, scope, roles, numbered steps with the reason for critical steps, visuals, a quality check and a revision date; each checked against its swimlane map.
plan_skeleton.brief: One action per step, starting with a verb. Screenshots or photos wherever a step involves a screen or a physical setup.

plan_skeleton.title: Automation candidates
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Every manual step scored by frequency, time and error risk; the top five automation candidates with hours saved per month and the connector each needs. Nothing is built in this recipe.
plan_skeleton.brief: Hand the list to the automation sweep recipe when the owner is ready.

plan_skeleton.title: SOP cold-read test
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES. Each SOP cold-read as a new hire would: ambiguous steps, missing controls, unowned steps and undefined terms listed with fixes.
plan_skeleton.brief: Read each SOP without the map or any context, then try to predict the output of the process.

plan_skeleton.title: Searchable process library
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A library organised by process with consistent naming, an owner and a review date for each SOP, and tags; search tested with ten real questions; a glossary of business-specific terms.
plan_skeleton.brief: Link each SOP to the decision records and memories it depends on so nothing contradicts.

meeting_moments.title: Which processes hurt most?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Lars asks where work gets stuck, redone or depends on one person, Morgan asks what you'd want a new hire to read first, and Dawit asks which mistakes cost the most. You leave with the eight processes to fix first.

meeting_moments.title: Process walk with the people who do the work
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Lars walks each swimlane with you (invite the person who does the work) and asks why at every wait and hand-off, while Felipe marks what could be automated later. You agree the improved way before it's written down.

meeting_moments.title: What to fix next
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: A short retro on which SOPs passed Dawit's cold read first time, which needed rework and why, and the next five processes to map. Frankie shows you how to find anything in the library.

duration_estimate.note: Needs about two hours of your team's time across the process walks.

lines: 14 core processes found; 5 are done three different ways by three people.
Priority 1: quote-to-invoice (weekly errors, 6 hours of rework).
Priority 2: new-client setup (every client asked for documents twice).
SIPOC and swimlane maps drafted for both; one improvement each agreed with the person who does the job.

success_criteria: Each of the top eight processes has a map and an SOP with a named owner and a review date.
Every SOP passes a cold read with no unowned or ambiguous steps.
The library returns the right SOP for at least 9 of 10 real test questions.
At least five automation candidates are sized in hours saved per month.

variants_by_industry.changes: Standard work, 5S audits and ISO 9001-style document control with controlled revisions.
Opening, closing, line checks, food-safety logs and station guides with photos.
Front-desk, billing and records SOPs. The team writes and changes nothing clinical.
Job-site setup, safety, daily logs and closeout procedures, with a voiced toolbox talk.
Pick-pack-ship, returns and stock-count procedures with SLA targets.
Client onboarding, delivery, QA and invoicing procedures with scope checkpoints.

recipes.name: Inventory & supplier tune-up
recipes.outcome: Reorder points, safety stock, supplier scorecards and a savings plan.
recipes.when_to_use: Your bestsellers run out while the rest sits on the shelf, suppliers are late more often than they should be, or too much cash is tied up in stock. You want reorder rules you can trust and a clear view of which suppliers are worth keeping.

inputs_from_owner.label: Twelve or more months of sales and inventory history (or connect your store or POS)
inputs_from_owner.example: Shopify orders and inventory levels

inputs_from_owner.label: Suppliers, their terms and lead times
inputs_from_owner.example: 6 suppliers; net-30; 2–6 week lead times

inputs_from_owner.label: A target in-stock rate or a limit on cash in inventory
inputs_from_owner.example: 95% in stock on the top 50 SKUs; under $120k in stock

inputs_from_owner.label: Storage, minimum-order or shelf-life constraints
inputs_from_owner.example: MOQ 200 units on apparel; one small warehouse

inputs_from_owner.label: Promotions, seasons or launches coming up
inputs_from_owner.example: Black Friday; a new colourway in February

composition.why: Mariam forecasts demand by SKU and sets reorder points, safety stock and order quantities that balance stockouts against cash.
Viktor scores suppliers on on-time-in-full, quality and cost, and builds the savings plan and RFQs.
Tendai works out the true landed cost and margin by SKU and supplier, so savings are real and not just a lower unit price.
Putri speaks for the stockout you didn't see coming. She backtests the reorder rules on real history and challenges the service level.

plan_skeleton.title: SKU demand forecast
plan_skeleton.acceptance: SKU-level (or SKU-family) demand for the next 13–26 weeks with seasonality, ABC/XYZ classes and forecast error (MAPE) on a holdout; stockout periods flagged so lost sales aren't mistaken for low demand.
plan_skeleton.brief: Group long-tail SKUs into families; forecast individually only where volume supports it.

plan_skeleton.title: Landed cost and margin by SKU
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Landed cost per SKU (unit price, freight, duty, handling and carrying cost) and margin by supplier; a total-cost-of-ownership comparison wherever an alternative supplier exists.
plan_skeleton.brief: Use real invoices and freight bills; mark any cost that has to be estimated.

plan_skeleton.title: Supplier scorecards
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Each key supplier scored on on-time-in-full, quality, lead time and its variability, price and responsiveness, from real purchase-order data; Kraljic position; red, amber or green with evidence.
plan_skeleton.brief: Lead-time variability matters as much as the average; report both.

plan_skeleton.title: Reorder points, safety stock and order quantities
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Reorder point, service-level-based safety stock (using lead-time variability) and order quantity (EOQ or min/max) for every SKU; cash in inventory before and after; the top overstock and stockout risks listed.
plan_skeleton.brief: Respect minimum order quantities and storage limits, and say where they force a trade-off.

plan_skeleton.title: Backtest and service-level challenge
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES. The reorder policy is replayed against the last 6–12 months to show the stockouts and cash it would have produced; the service-level choice is defended or changed.
plan_skeleton.brief: Replay week by week with actual demand and actual lead times.

plan_skeleton.title: Supplier savings plan
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Ranked savings opportunities (renegotiate, consolidate, dual-source or re-quote) with estimated annual savings, supply risk and a first step; RFQ drafts prepared but not sent.
plan_skeleton.brief: Never trade a strategic supplier's reliability for a small unit-price saving without saying so.

deliverables.name: Demand forecast and reorder policy by SKU
Landed cost and margin by SKU
RFQ drafts
deliverables.description: Prepared for approval; nothing is sent automatically.

meeting_moments.title: Inventory kickoff
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Mariam names the SKUs that run out and the ones gathering dust, Viktor names the suppliers causing the most pain, and Putri asks which months of data we shouldn't trust. You set the in-stock target and the cash limit.

meeting_moments.title: Service level versus cash
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Putri replays last year with the new rules: here are the four weeks we'd still have run out, and here's the cash we'd have freed. Mariam and Tendai adjust, and you hear the trade-off in plain numbers.

meeting_moments.title: Which suppliers to renegotiate
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Viktor gives the top three savings moves with the risk of each, and Mariam confirms the reorder rules going live. You approve which RFQs go out.

duration_estimate.note: Reorder rules then refresh monthly in about 20 minutes.

lines: A items: 18 SKUs are 71% of sales; 4 stocked out last quarter.
Reorder point for SKU-114: 62 units (lead time 12 days, safety stock 18).
9 C items hold 14k of cash that turns less than twice a year: stop reordering.
Supplier B is 11% cheaper landed but late 1 in 5 times: keep A for A items.

success_criteria: Every active SKU has a reorder point, safety stock and order quantity, with its assumptions shown.
Replayed against the last 6–12 months, the policy shows fewer stockout weeks at equal or lower average inventory cash, or the trade-off is explained.
Every key supplier has a scorecard built from real purchase-order data.
Savings are stated as annual amounts with a supply-risk rating, and no RFQ goes out without approval.

variants_by_industry.changes: Perishables: par levels by day of the week, waste tracking and recipe-driven usage from the menu mix.
Multilevel BOMs and MRP: weekly planned orders with lead-time offsets and shortage flags.
Marketplace restock limits, inbound shipment planning and 3PL storage fees in the reorder math.
Job-driven materials: long-lead items tied to the project schedule, and supplier quotes per bid.
Van and truck stock: a standard van list per job type, restocking by zone and a monthly count.

recipes.name: Customer support desk setup
recipes.outcome: A ticket taxonomy, SLAs, macro library, top-20 help articles and a QA scorecard.
recipes.when_to_use: Support is a shared inbox and good intentions. Replies depend on who answers, the same questions arrive every day, and you can't tell whether customers are getting good help. You want a desk that runs to a standard from day one.

inputs_from_owner.label: The support channels you use
inputs_from_owner.example: Email, Instagram DMs, website chat

inputs_from_owner.label: A recent export or sample of customer conversations
inputs_from_owner.example: The last 3 months of Gmail support threads

inputs_from_owner.label: Support hours and who answers
inputs_from_owner.example: Weekdays 9–5; me and one part-timer

inputs_from_owner.label: Your helpdesk tool, if any (or connect it)
inputs_from_owner.example: Gorgias trial; mostly Gmail

inputs_from_owner.label: How you want to sound
inputs_from_owner.example: Friendly, straight, never corporate

inputs_from_owner.label: Complaints you already know about
inputs_from_owner.example: 'Where's my order?' and sizing questions

composition.why: Bongani designs the desk: contact-reason taxonomy, SLAs, escalation paths and a staffing plan that meets them.
Paloma writes the top-20 help articles in KCS style, so customers solve the common problems themselves.
Ravi builds the macro library and a weighted QA scorecard, then calibrates it on real conversations.
Felipe sets up routing, tagging and SLA timers in your helpdesk, tested before anything goes live.
Ruth speaks for the frustrated customer at 11pm, running difficult scenarios through the macros and articles until nothing reads cold or wrong.

plan_skeleton.title: Contact-reason taxonomy from real tickets
plan_skeleton.acceptance: The last 90 days of tickets, emails and DMs sampled; a two-level contact-reason taxonomy with 25 or fewer leaves, showing volume, handle time and channel; the top 20 reasons cover at least 80% of volume, or the gap is stated.
plan_skeleton.brief: Strip customer personal data from any examples kept in the taxonomy.

plan_skeleton.title: SLAs, escalation and staffing
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First-response and resolution SLAs by priority and channel; business hours and escalation paths; staffing need by hour from the volume pattern (Erlang-C style), with the SLA it achieves.
plan_skeleton.brief: Set SLAs the current team can meet on a bad week, then show what extra capacity would buy.

plan_skeleton.title: Top-20 help articles
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Top-20 task-based help articles in KCS format, each titled as the customer's question, with steps, screenshot placeholders and a 'still stuck?' route; nothing is published without owner approval.
plan_skeleton.brief: Write in the customer's words from the tickets, not in internal jargon.

plan_skeleton.title: Macro library
plan_skeleton.acceptance: One macro per top contact reason, with personalisation slots, an empathy line, the fix and the next step; each links to its help article; the tone matches the brand voice.
plan_skeleton.brief: Every macro must read well with the personalisation slots left blank, so there are no 'Hi {name}' accidents.

plan_skeleton.title: Helpdesk routing and SLA timers
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Routing, tagging, priority and SLA timers designed for the owner's helpdesk or shared inbox, with test cases; built in test mode and switched on only after owner approval.
plan_skeleton.brief: If there's no helpdesk yet, design the rules for a shared inbox and flag the point where a helpdesk pays for itself.

plan_skeleton.title: QA scorecard and calibration
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A weighted QA rubric (accuracy, resolution, tone, process) with critical-error gates; ten sample conversations scored for calibration; a coaching-note template.
plan_skeleton.brief: Critical errors (wrong refund, privacy slip, a promise ops can't keep) fail the review regardless of score.

plan_skeleton.title: Frustrated-customer test
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES. Five angry, confused or edge-case customer scenarios are run through the macros and articles; every dead end, cold reply or wrong answer is listed with a fix.
plan_skeleton.brief: Include a customer who has already written in three times and one who writes in a second language.

meeting_moments.title: Support kickoff
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Bongani shares the top contact reasons from your inbox, Paloma picks the questions a good article would stop, Ravi asks what 'a great reply' means to you, and Ruth asks what your angriest customer said last month.

meeting_moments.title: Would a frustrated customer feel helped?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Ruth plays five difficult customers live against the new macros and articles, and Ravi and Paloma fix them on the spot. You hear exactly what your customers would have experienced.

meeting_moments.title: How your desk works now
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Bongani explains the SLAs, the staffing need and the escalation path in three minutes, and Felipe describes the routing rules waiting for your approval.

lines: Top reasons (last 90 days): 'where is my order' 31%, returns 18%, sizing 12%.
First-response SLA: 2 business hours for email, 5 minutes for chat.
12 macros cover 64% of tickets; each is personalised before sending.
Top-20 help articles planned from the real questions.

success_criteria: The top 20 contact reasons cover at least 80% of volume, and each has a macro and a help article.
SLAs are defined by priority and channel, and the staffing plan meets them on paper.
The QA rubric has been calibrated on ten real conversations.
No help article is published and no routing rule switched on without the owner's approval.
Every failure found in the frustrated-customer test has a logged fix.

variants_by_industry.changes: WISMO deflection with tracking links, returns and exchange macros, and order lookup in the helpdesk.
Bug and feature-request routing to product, in-app help and a tiered escalation to engineering.
Reservations, private events and public review responses in the same desk.
Administrative questions only. Anything clinical goes to the practice's clinicians with a safe holding reply.
Community and membership support with forum moderation and escalation to safety.
Phones first: missed-call text-back, a booking script and after-hours replies; texts only to consented contacts.

recipes.name: Churn rescue
recipes.outcome: A churn diagnosis, at-risk list with save plays, a fair cancellation flow and win-back sequence.
recipes.when_to_use: Customers or members are leaving faster than you can replace them, and you're not sure why. You want to know who is at risk right now, what would keep them, a cancellation experience that's fair (and legal), and a way to win some back.

inputs_from_owner.label: Subscription or membership data (connect billing or export it)
inputs_from_owner.example: Stripe subscriptions export

inputs_from_owner.label: Cancellation reasons, surveys, tickets or reviews
inputs_from_owner.example: Cancel-survey answers in Typeform; Zendesk tickets

inputs_from_owner.label: How cancelling works today and any offers you make
inputs_from_owner.example: Customers email us to cancel; we sometimes offer a free month

inputs_from_owner.label: Where your customers are, for auto-renewal and consumer-protection rules
inputs_from_owner.example: US and UK

inputs_from_owner.label: What you could offer: a pause, a downgrade, a discount or a fix
inputs_from_owner.example: Pause for up to 3 months; a cheaper plan

composition.why: Hana builds the health score and the at-risk list, with a named save play for every account worth saving.
Hélène designs a cancellation flow that is as easy as signing up, with at most one relevant save offer and a clean goodbye.
Taras codes cancellation reasons, tickets and reviews into a churn-reason taxonomy with real customer words.
Ahmad speaks for the margin. He cuts any save offer that costs more than the customer is worth or teaches people to threaten to cancel.
Anneke checks the cancellation flow and save offers against auto-renewal and consumer-protection rules where your customers live, and prepares the licensed review.
Sebastián makes sure win-back messages go only to people who can lawfully receive them and that churn data stays minimal.

plan_skeleton.title: Retention by cohort
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Logo and revenue retention by signup cohort, plan and channel; churn split into voluntary and involuntary (failed payments); the month with the biggest drop-off identified.
plan_skeleton.brief: Work from billing data. Show the curve, and not only an average churn rate.

plan_skeleton.title: Churn-reason taxonomy
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Cancellation reasons, tickets and survey comments coded into a churn-reason taxonomy with counts and verbatim quotes; reasons split into controllable and uncontrollable.
plan_skeleton.brief: Quotes are anonymized; keep only what's needed to understand the reason.

plan_skeleton.title: At-risk list and save plays
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A health score from usage, support and payment signals; current accounts ranked by risk × value, each with a named save play and owner; no outreach is sent.
plan_skeleton.brief: Save plays fix the reason where possible (onboarding help, a product fix) before offering a discount.

plan_skeleton.title: Fair cancellation and save flow
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A cancel path as easy as sign-up: reason capture, at most one relevant save offer (pause, downgrade or fix) and a clear confirmation; dunning steps for involuntary churn; flagged against auto-renewal and consumer-protection rules for each market.
plan_skeleton.brief: No confirmshaming, hidden links or forced phone calls. The customer can always finish cancelling in the same channel they started in.

plan_skeleton.title: Save-offer economics
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES. Each save offer is costed against customer lifetime value and payback; offers that lose money or reward threats to cancel are cut.
plan_skeleton.brief: Model take-rate scenarios. An offer that works for 10% of cancellers can still lose money on the other 90%.

plan_skeleton.title: Win-back sequence
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A win-back sequence of three to four emails per churn reason, with timing, offer rules, suppression and consent checks, and subject-line tests; loaded only after owner approval.
plan_skeleton.brief: Only contact people who agreed to marketing, and lead with what changed rather than a discount.

plan_skeleton.title: Licensed review of cancellation and renewal terms
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Counsel has reviewed the cancellation flow, the renewal disclosures and the save-offer terms for the owner's markets; changes are applied; nothing goes live before the owner approves.
plan_skeleton.brief: Anneke packages the cancellation flow, save offers and renewal terms with the applicable rules for counsel, and Sebastián adds the consent basis for win-back messages; each decision is recorded.

meeting_moments.title: Churn kickoff
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Hana frames the question of who leaves, when and why. Camila shares the first retention curve, Taras reads three real cancellation comments aloud, and Hélène asks what you're willing to offer someone on their way out.

meeting_moments.title: Which save offers are worth it?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Ahmad shows which offers keep customers worth keeping and which just teach people to threaten to cancel, and Hélène defends the ones that fix the real reason. You hear which offers survive and why.

meeting_moments.title: Your churn rescue plan
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Hana reads out the top ten at-risk accounts and their save plays, Hélène walks through the new cancellation flow, and Hamish previews the first win-back email. You approve what goes live after counsel's review.

duration_estimate.note: Counsel's review time comes on top.

lines: Monthly logo churn 4.8%; 38% is involuntary (failed payments).
Top voluntary reason: 'didn't get set up' (41%); most leave in month 2.
Save offers pay back only for plans above 60 a month; below that, fix onboarding instead.
Cancellation stays one click; win-back emails go only to people who can lawfully receive them.

success_criteria: Churn is split into voluntary and involuntary, with retention curves by cohort.
Every at-risk account has a named save play and an owner.
Cancelling takes no more steps than signing up and shows at most one relevant save offer.
Every save offer pays back within the customer's expected lifetime, or it is cut.
Counsel has reviewed the cancellation and renewal terms, and nothing goes live or is sent without the owner's approval.

variants_by_industry.changes: Membership freezes, falling class attendance as the early signal, and front-desk save conversations.
Subscription boxes and replenishment: skip or swap before cancel, plus loyalty tiers.
Product-usage health scores, activation gaps and seat contraction as signals.
Cohort programs and coaching packages: mid-program drop-off and completion nudges.
Paid communities and memberships: engagement rituals and a community-led save.
Maintenance-plan members: renewal reminders before the busy season, a visit-completion check and a save offer that reschedules the visit rather than discounting.

recipes.name: Internal tool build
recipes.outcome: A working internal tool (tracker, calculator, portal) built in the app canvas and documented.
recipes.when_to_use: An important part of the business runs on a spreadsheet, whiteboard or sticky notes, and it's breaking: double entry, lost updates, and nobody knows which version is current. You want a small, solid internal tool (a tracker, calculator or portal) built and documented.

inputs_from_owner.example: Track jobs from quote to invoice for 4 office staff

inputs_from_owner.label: The spreadsheet or process it replaces
inputs_from_owner.example: Jobs.xlsx with 11 tabs

inputs_from_owner.example: Quotes from Jobber, invoices to QuickBooks

inputs_from_owner.example: Techs see their own jobs; the office edits everything

composition.why: Kareem builds the tool in the sandboxed canvas as small, reviewable steps, with input validation and a clean data export.
Nikos writes the one-page PRD with testable acceptance criteria and runs your sign-off against them.

plan_skeleton.title: One-page PRD
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A one-page PRD covering users, the job the tool does, the current workaround and what it costs, must-have fields and screens, data sources, permissions and testable acceptance criteria, plus an out-of-scope list.
