plan_skeleton.title: Clickable wireframes
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Clickable wireframes of every must-have screen and the main flow, including empty, error and loading states; the owner can click through them in the canvas.

plan_skeleton.title: Build the tool
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A working tool in the sandboxed canvas with real or sample data, input validation and CSV export; no credentials stored in the app; every acceptance criterion can be demonstrated.

plan_skeleton.title: Test plan and bug bash
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES. Test cases for every acceptance criterion, including edge cases (empty data, duplicates, large lists, bad input); bugs logged with reproduction steps and retested after fixes.

plan_skeleton.title: User guide, reference and admin notes
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A how-to guide for users, a reference of fields and rules, an admin page on data and backups, and a changelog, split the Diátaxis way, with screenshots of the real tool.
plan_skeleton.brief: Write the how-to guide for someone who has never seen the tool, and test it on them if possible.

plan_skeleton.title: Owner acceptance walkthrough
plan_skeleton.acceptance: The owner has walked through the tool against each acceptance criterion, and the sign-off or change list is recorded.
plan_skeleton.brief: Nikos runs the walkthrough criterion by criterion, and anything not demonstrated doesn't count.

deliverables.description: Runs in the sandboxed canvas with validation and CSV export.

meeting_moments.title: Show us the spreadsheet you hate

meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Kareem demos the working tool against each acceptance criterion, Pilar reports what she tried to break and what's fixed, and Morgan shows where the guide lives. You sign off or list changes.

lines: Job: track quotes from request to won or lost, replacing the whiteboard and 3 spreadsheets.

Done means: the owner can find any quote in under 10 seconds.

success_criteria: Every must-have acceptance criterion passes in the owner's walkthrough.
The test plan covers empty, duplicate, large and invalid data, and no critical bug is left open.
The tool stores no credentials and can export all of its data to CSV.
Someone who has never seen the tool can complete the main task using only the guide.

variants_by_industry.changes: A job tracker or estimate calculator with change orders and a site-photo log.
A transaction tracker with contract-to-close milestones and party checklists.
A prep-list and ordering calculator driven by forecast covers and recipes.
A utilization and project-budget tracker with a weekly timesheet import.
A donor and volunteer tracker with a stewardship calendar.
A matter-intake tracker with conflict-check status and deadlines; docketing stays in the firm's system of record.

recipes.name: MVP prototype
recipes.outcome: A PRD, a clickable or working prototype, and a usability test with findings.
recipes.when_to_use: You have an idea for a new product, feature or service and want to find out if it's worth building, with a real prototype in front of real people, before you spend months or a developer budget on it.

inputs_from_owner.label: The idea and who it's for
inputs_from_owner.example: A booking app for mobile dog groomers

inputs_from_owner.label: Five to eight people who could be interviewed or test it
inputs_from_owner.example: Six regular clients and two groomers I know

inputs_from_owner.label: Evidence so far: customer requests, notes, emails, competitors
inputs_from_owner.example: 12 customers asked for online booking this year

inputs_from_owner.label: Budget, deadline or must-integrate constraints
inputs_from_owner.example: Must work on phones and sync with Google Calendar

inputs_from_owner.label: What result would convince you to build it
inputs_from_owner.example: 4 of 6 testers book without help and say they'd use it

composition.why: Nikos turns the idea into a problem-first PRD and a story map with the thinnest end-to-end slice worth testing.
Tariq builds the clickable or working prototype in the canvas, faking whatever doesn't need to be real yet.
Hina designs the flows mobile-first and decides with Tariq what gets faked and what gets built.
Dilani runs the JTBD interviews and the usability test, and plays back what people did rather than what they said.
Esther speaks for the evidence. She sets the success and stop thresholds before anything is built and holds the team to them.

plan_skeleton.title: Problem interviews and synthesis
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A JTBD interview guide, plus a synthesis of five to eight conversations (run by the owner, or from recordings and notes they supply) into forces of progress; the job, the struggling moment and today's alternatives, each backed by quotes.
plan_skeleton.brief: Ask about the last time the problem happened, never about whether they'd like the idea.

plan_skeleton.title: Success and stop thresholds
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Before anything is built: the decision this prototype informs, the success and stop thresholds (such as task success rate, stated intent or fake-door clicks), the sample size and the result that would stop the project.
plan_skeleton.brief: Small-sample tests give directional evidence only. Say so, and set the thresholds accordingly.

plan_skeleton.title: PRD and story map
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A PRD covering problem, target user, success metric, scope and testable acceptance criteria, plus a story map with the thinnest end-to-end release slice marked.
plan_skeleton.brief: Cut the slice until it feels too small, then test it.

plan_skeleton.title: User flows and wireframes
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A user flow and wireframes for the MVP slice, mobile-first; the decision on what is faked (Wizard-of-Oz) and what is built is recorded.
plan_skeleton.brief: Design the moment of value first and the sign-up last.

plan_skeleton.title: Prototype build
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A clickable or working prototype in the canvas that covers the core job end to end, with faked parts clearly marked internally and a shareable test link; any fake door is honest, says the feature is coming, and takes no payment.
plan_skeleton.brief: Build only what the test needs. Everything else can be a convincing placeholder.

plan_skeleton.title: Usability test
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES. Five tasks with success criteria; sessions run with the owner's testers (live, or from recordings they supply); findings by severity with quotes; results compared with the pre-agreed thresholds.
plan_skeleton.brief: Testers' personal data is kept to first names and minimized in notes.

plan_skeleton.title: Build, iterate or stop decision
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Findings ranked with RICE; a build, iterate or stop recommendation measured against the pre-agreed thresholds; the owner's decision recorded.
plan_skeleton.brief: If the results are ambiguous, recommend the cheapest next test rather than a build.

deliverables.name: PRD with success and stop thresholds
Story map with the MVP slice

meeting_moments.title: MVP kickoff
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Nikos restates the idea as a problem, Dilani asks who struggles with it most, Esther asks what result would make you stop, and Tariq says what he could fake by Friday. Ten minutes that set the evidence bar before anyone falls in love with a solution.

meeting_moments.title: Three ways to fake it
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Tariq and Hina brainstorm the cheapest honest ways to test the core job (a clickable flow, a concierge version, a fake door), and Esther asks which one actually answers the question. You pick one.

meeting_moments.title: What the testers told us
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Dilani plays back the key moments from each session, Esther scores the results against the bar you set, and Nikos proposes build, iterate or stop. You hear the evidence before you decide.

duration_estimate.note: Calendar time depends mostly on when your testers are available.

lines: Decision: build the booking app, iterate, or stop.
Success: 4 of 5 testers book without help in under 2 minutes; 3 of 5 say they would switch.
Stop: fewer than 2 of 5 complete the core task after one iteration.
Interview synthesis: the push is last-minute cancellations, not booking itself.

success_criteria: The success and stop thresholds were written down before the prototype was built.
The prototype covers the core job end to end and has been tested with at least five people.
Every usability finding has a severity rating and a supporting quote or observation.
The build, iterate or stop decision cites the pre-agreed thresholds and is recorded.
Any fake-door test was honest and took no payments.

variants_by_industry.changes: Adds a fake door on the pricing page and activation metrics for the new feature. If the product is an app, Nasrin checks offline behaviour and store readiness from the first prototype.
A new product line: a pre-order landing page with honest 'coming soon' messaging and demand tracking.
A course MVP: a pilot lesson and outline tested with a small cohort before the full build.
A patient-facing admin tool (booking, forms). Non-clinical only, accessibility-tested, and privacy-reviewed before any real patient data is used.
A class-booking or member-app prototype tested with members at the front desk.

recipes.name: KPI tree & dashboard
recipes.outcome: Agreed metric definitions, a KPI tree and a live dashboard with alert thresholds.
recipes.when_to_use: You check five apps and a spreadsheet to find out how the business is doing, the numbers disagree with each other, and nothing warns you when something is going wrong. You want agreed definitions, one screen, and alerts that only fire when it matters.

inputs_from_owner.label: The decisions you make every week or month
inputs_from_owner.example: How much to spend on ads; whether to hire; which products to push

inputs_from_owner.label: The systems that hold the numbers (or enable connectors)
inputs_from_owner.example: Shopify, QuickBooks, Google Analytics, Klaviyo

inputs_from_owner.label: Reports or spreadsheets you use today
inputs_from_owner.example: The Monday numbers spreadsheet

inputs_from_owner.label: Targets you already have
inputs_from_owner.example: $1.2M revenue; 45% gross margin

inputs_from_owner.label: Who should get alerts, and how
inputs_from_owner.example: Me on Slack; the ops manager for stock alerts

composition.why: Rashid starts from your decisions, builds the KPI tree and writes a definition, owner and source for every metric.
Hugo builds the one-screen dashboard, following Tufte and Few, so every chart answers exactly one question.
Rustam traces every metric to its source, builds read-only imports with data-quality tests, and wires the alerts.
Ingrid ties the surviving metrics to your goals so the dashboard and the plan tell the same story.
Carmen speaks for the person who has to act on the number. If a metric moving wouldn't change a decision, it goes.

plan_skeleton.title: KPI tree and metric definitions
plan_skeleton.acceptance: An outcome metric at the top, three to five drivers and input metrics below; every metric has a written definition, formula, source system, owner, cadence and the decision it informs.
plan_skeleton.brief: Start from the owner's weekly decisions and work backwards to the metrics.

plan_skeleton.title: Metric challenge
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES. Every metric passes the test 'what would we do differently if it moved?'; vanity metrics are cut; each lagging metric is paired with a leading one.
plan_skeleton.brief: Carmen challenges each metric aloud, and the survivors go to the build.

plan_skeleton.title: Source audit and data model
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Each metric traced to its source; gaps, duplicates and definition conflicts listed; read-only scheduled imports into tidy tables with freshness, null and duplicate tests; last month's key figures reconcile to the source of truth within a stated tolerance.
plan_skeleton.brief: Read-only access everywhere. Any change to a source system is a separate, approved task.

plan_skeleton.title: Live dashboard
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A one-screen dashboard that follows the KPI tree top-down; each chart answers one question; definitions on hover; targets and the prior period shown; accessible colours; live connector data.
plan_skeleton.brief: Start with the answer, not the data: the most important number goes top-left.

plan_skeleton.title: Alert thresholds
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Threshold and anomaly rules for each key metric, naming who is alerted and what they do; backtested on the last 90 days to keep false alarms under one a week; switched on only after owner approval.
plan_skeleton.brief: Every alert says what to check first, or it doesn't ship.

plan_skeleton.title: First weekly voiced readout
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A two-minute voiced weekly readout generated from the live dashboard (what moved, why, and what needs attention), with every number matching the screen.
plan_skeleton.brief: Pyramid Principle: the answer first, then the three reasons.

meeting_moments.title: Which decisions do you make every week?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Rashid starts from your decisions, not your data: what you decide each week and what you'd need to know to decide better. Carmen asks what you'd actually do if a number turned red, and Hugo sketches the screen as you talk.

meeting_moments.title: Keep, cut or redefine?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Rashid chairs while Carmen challenges each metric: if this moved, what would you do? Ingrid ties the survivors to your goals and Rustam says which ones the data can actually support. Fewer, better numbers come out.

meeting_moments.title: Your first weekly readout
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Rashid plays the first two-minute readout from the live dashboard, and Hugo shows where each number lives on screen. This is what you'll hear every Monday.

lines: Outcome: monthly gross profit. Drivers: jobs completed, average job value, gross margin.
Inputs: quotes sent, quote win rate, callback rate.
Cut: 'website visits' (no one acts on it).
Every metric has a formula, a source, an owner and a red/green rule.

success_criteria: Every metric on the dashboard has a written definition, a source, an owner and the decision it informs.
Last month's key figures on the dashboard reconcile to the source of truth within the stated tolerance.
Every alert names a recipient and an action, and the backtest shows fewer than one false alarm a week.
The owner can answer 'how are we doing?' from one screen in under a minute.

variants_by_industry.changes: MRR, NRR, activation, burn multiple and CAC payback on the tree.
MER, contribution margin per order, repeat rate and inventory weeks of cover.
Covers, average check, prime cost and labor percentage by daypart.
Utilization, realization, pipeline coverage and retainer health.
OEE, scrap, on-time delivery and changeover time.
Program outcomes, cost per outcome, donor retention and the burn rate on restricted funds.

recipes.name: Security hardening sprint
recipes.outcome: A threat model, CIS IG1 gap check, access review, backup plan and incident runbook.
recipes.when_to_use: You've never taken a proper look at security, or a client, insurer or near-miss has just shown you that you should. You want to know what's actually exposed, fix the basics in the right order, and know exactly what to do if something goes wrong.

inputs_from_owner.label: Your apps and devices and who uses them (or let us read enabled connectors)
inputs_from_owner.example: Google Workspace, QuickBooks, Shopify, 8 laptops, staff phones

inputs_from_owner.label: Where your most important data lives
inputs_from_owner.example: Customer list in HubSpot, financials in QuickBooks, designs on Dropbox

inputs_from_owner.label: How things are backed up today
inputs_from_owner.example: Whatever Google does by default; nothing else

inputs_from_owner.label: Past incidents or near-misses
inputs_from_owner.example: An invoice-fraud email almost got paid last year

inputs_from_owner.label: Anyone asking you about security (clients, insurer, regulator)
inputs_from_owner.example: Cyber insurance renewal questionnaire

inputs_from_owner.label: Your IT or security provider, if any
inputs_from_owner.example: A local MSP on call

composition.why: Hafsa leads the sprint: STRIDE threat model, the CIS Controls IG1 gap check and the incident runbook, all defensive and in plain language.
Precious inventories your apps, devices and admin accounts and runs the access review, proposing changes but never making them without approval.
Pavel makes sure you can recover: 3-2-1 backups, RTO and RPO targets and a real restore test.
Jelena thinks like the attacker who isn't in the room. She pre-mortems the plan from the breach backwards and finds the paths it misses.
Martina checks the asset inventory and access review for evidence you could show a customer or insurer, and flags where personal data lives.

plan_skeleton.title: Asset and data inventory
plan_skeleton.acceptance: An inventory of devices, SaaS apps, admin accounts and data stores with an owner for each; the crown-jewel data identified; unknown or unmanaged items flagged.
plan_skeleton.brief: Read admin settings and connector metadata only. Never collect passwords or secrets.

plan_skeleton.title: STRIDE threat model
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A data-flow diagram of the business's key systems; STRIDE threats for each element ranked by likelihood × impact; the top ten mitigations mapped to CIS safeguards.
plan_skeleton.brief: Focus on what really happens to small businesses: phishing, account takeover, invoice fraud, ransomware and lost devices.

plan_skeleton.title: CIS Controls IG1 gap check
plan_skeleton.acceptance: All 56 CIS Controls v8 IG1 safeguards marked met, partial or not met, with evidence; a 30/60/90-day fix plan ordered by risk reduction per hour of effort.
plan_skeleton.brief: Quick wins first: MFA everywhere, a password manager, automatic updates and admin separation.

plan_skeleton.title: Access review
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Every user and admin in the key apps reviewed against their role, with MFA status; stale, shared and over-privileged accounts listed with a proposed change; no access is changed without owner approval.
plan_skeleton.brief: Include former staff, contractors and integration accounts, since they are the ones most often missed.

plan_skeleton.title: Backup and disaster-recovery plan
plan_skeleton.acceptance: 3-2-1 backup coverage for each crown-jewel system with RPO and RTO targets; at least one restore test completed, or scheduled with the owner and dated; gaps listed with costed fixes.
plan_skeleton.brief: SaaS data is not automatically backed up in a way you control; check each system's export and retention.

plan_skeleton.title: Incident response runbook
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A runbook for the top five incident types (phishing or account takeover, ransomware, lost device, vendor breach, data leak) covering detect, contain, communicate and recover, with contacts and decision rights, plus a one-page wallet card.
plan_skeleton.brief: Write it for the owner at 11pm on a Saturday, not for a security team.

plan_skeleton.title: Attacker's-eye pre-mortem
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES. A pre-mortem from the attacker's side ('it's six months from now and we were breached; how?') tests the plan, and any unaddressed path is added to the fix list.
plan_skeleton.brief: Defensive reasoning only. No exploit development, and no testing against systems the owner doesn't control.

plan_skeleton.title: Licensed review of high-risk changes by a qualified security professional
plan_skeleton.acceptance: High-risk changes (admin access removal, MFA enforcement, backup re-architecture) are reviewed by a qualified security professional where the owner has one, and approved by the owner; each change is scheduled with a rollback.
plan_skeleton.brief: Where the owner has no security professional, Hafsa says so plainly and recommends which changes justify bringing one in.

deliverables.name: Incident response runbook and wallet card

meeting_moments.title: Security kickoff
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Hafsa explains what 'crown jewels' means for your business, Precious lists what she found in your accounts, Pavel asks when you last restored a backup, and Jelena asks how she'd get in if she were an attacker. No jargon and no scare tactics.

meeting_moments.title: Tabletop: a phishing email got through
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Hafsa runs a 15-minute tabletop with you: your bookkeeper has just entered her password on a fake login page. What happens next? You answer, and the team shows where the runbook helps and where it still has gaps.

meeting_moments.title: Red-team read-out
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Jelena presents the three most likely ways the business gets breached six months from now, and whether the plan stops each one. You hear which fixes to make this week.

duration_estimate.note: The fixes themselves roll out over 30, 60 and 90 days, each one approved.

lines: 31 apps found; 9 have no named owner; 2 former staff still have access.
MFA missing on email for 4 of 11 accounts, including the owner's admin account.
Fix-before-coffee: remove leaver access and turn on MFA (you approve each change).
Backups: files are backed up, but the booking system has never been restore-tested.

success_criteria: Every crown-jewel system has a named owner, MFA status, backup coverage and RTO and RPO targets.
All 56 CIS Controls v8 IG1 safeguards are marked met, partial or not met, with evidence.
Every stale, shared or over-privileged account is listed with a proposed change, and none is changed without approval.
At least one restore test is completed, or scheduled with a date.
The runbook covers the top five incident types and has been walked through in a tabletop.

variants_by_industry.changes: HIPAA Security Rule risk-analysis flags, an ePHI inventory and BAAs, and workforce access by role.
Client confidentiality, trust-account payment-fraud controls and access by matter.
Adds cloud and CI secrets, production access and a SOC 2 readiness path.
Separating client data, and answering client security questionnaires consistently.
Store admin access, payment-page scripts, minimizing PCI scope and refund-fraud controls.

recipes.name: Automation sweep
recipes.outcome: A ranked list of automation opportunities and the top three built, tested and approved.
recipes.when_to_use: You and your team spend hours each week copying data between tools, chasing the same reminders and rebuilding the same reports. You want the biggest time-wasters found and the top three automated properly (tested, safe and approved), not a fragile mess of automations nobody understands.

inputs_from_owner.label: The tools and connectors you use
inputs_from_owner.example: Gmail, HubSpot, QuickBooks, Google Sheets, Slack

inputs_from_owner.label: Anything that must never be automated
inputs_from_owner.example: Payments, and anything sent to customers without a human check

inputs_from_owner.label: Tasks you or your team repeat every week (a rough list is fine)
inputs_from_owner.example: Copy web leads into HubSpot; Friday invoice reminders; the Monday sales sheet

inputs_from_owner.label: Who does this work today, and roughly how long it takes
inputs_from_owner.example: The office manager, about 6 hours a week

inputs_from_owner.label: Your preferred automation platform, if any
inputs_from_owner.example: Zapier (we already have a plan)

composition.why: Felipe finds and sizes the opportunities, then designs and builds trigger-action flows with idempotent steps, retries and alerts.
Lars removes the waste before anything is automated, so you never automate a bad process, and chairs the pick-the-top-three decision.
Luz checks every connector for least-privilege scopes and safe data flows, and handles the go-live.
Pilar tests each automation against the happy path, bad data, duplicate events and a connector outage.
Walter speaks for the person who inherits this in two years. He asks who owns each automation, how you'll know it broke, and whether a simpler one would last longer.

plan_skeleton.title: Automation opportunity scan
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Repetitive tasks gathered from the owner, the team and connector activity; each scored by frequency × minutes × error cost ÷ build effort; a ranked list of at least ten with hours saved per month.
plan_skeleton.brief: Include the owner's 'never automate' list as a hard filter.

plan_skeleton.title: Fix the process before automating
plan_skeleton.acceptance: The top five candidates mapped; waste removed before automation (steps deleted or simplified); the simplified process each automation will follow written down.
plan_skeleton.brief: Often the best automation is a deleted step.

plan_skeleton.title: Design the top three
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Trigger-action designs for the top three, with idempotency, retries, error alerts and a manual fallback; least-privilege scopes for each connector; the data each one touches listed.
plan_skeleton.brief: Design so that running the same trigger twice never produces two records, two emails or two invoices.

plan_skeleton.title: Build in test mode
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Each automation built in test mode on sample data; the run logs show a success, a forced failure and a duplicate trigger all handled correctly; nothing runs live yet.
plan_skeleton.brief: Use test records and sandbox connections wherever the platform allows.

plan_skeleton.title: Automation test pass
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES. Test cases for the happy path, bad data, duplicate events and a connector outage for each automation, with results logged.
plan_skeleton.brief: Pilar tries to break each automation the way real life will.

plan_skeleton.title: Durability and ownership review
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES. For each automation: who owns it, how you'll know it broke, what it costs to run, and a one-page runbook a non-engineer can follow; brittle steps replaced.
plan_skeleton.brief: Prefer boring, well-documented steps over clever ones.

plan_skeleton.title: Approved go-live
plan_skeleton.acceptance: The owner approves each automation individually (scopes, schedule and rollback) before it goes live; a first-week monitoring check is set; the hours-saved baseline is recorded.
plan_skeleton.brief: One automation at a time, with a named owner watching the first week.

meeting_moments.title: What do you do every week that a robot should?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Felipe asks where your week goes, Lars asks why each step exists at all, and Walter asks what happened the last time an automation broke. You'll hear your list turned into hours.

meeting_moments.title: Pick the top three
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Lars chairs. Felipe pitches each design with the hours it saves, Luz says what access it needs, and Walter says how it could break. You choose the three to build.

meeting_moments.title: Will it still work next year?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Walter and Pilar report what they tried to break (duplicate triggers, bad data, an expired login) and what Felipe changed. You hear who owns each automation and how you'll know if it stops.

lines: 1. Copying web enquiries into the CRM: 3.5 hours a week, easy build, low risk.
2. Weekly job report: 3 hours a week; a spreadsheet formula removes most of it before any automation.
3. Invoice reminders: 2 hours a week; runs under a standing grant with a kill switch.
Each is fixed before it is automated, and each has a named owner.

success_criteria: At least ten opportunities are ranked by hours saved per month against build effort.
Waste was removed from each of the top three processes before automating, and each simplified process is written down.
In testing, every automation handles failure, duplicate and bad-data cases, and each has a runbook and a named owner.
No automation goes live until the owner has approved its scopes and rollback.
Hours saved are measured against the baseline after the first month.

variants_by_industry.changes: Lead follow-up, showing reminders and a transaction-milestone tracker.
Order exceptions, low-stock alerts, review requests and returns routing.
Time capture, invoice drafting and client status updates.
Intake, conflict-check requests and deadline reminders; docketing stays in the system of record.
Appointment reminders, waitlist fills and intake routing using minimum-necessary data.
Supplier orders from par levels, a daily sales recap and review alerts.

recipes.name: Crisis response room
recipes.outcome: A holding statement, stakeholder plan, operational fixes and a post-mortem, fast.
recipes.when_to_use: Something has gone wrong in public or is about to: a product problem, a data incident, an outage, a viral complaint or a safety issue. You need the facts straight, the right words out fast, the people who matter told in the right order, and the actual problem fixed.

inputs_from_owner.label: What happened, in your words, plus any evidence
inputs_from_owner.example: Customers are posting photos of mould in jars from batch 214

inputs_from_owner.label: Who is affected, and roughly how many
inputs_from_owner.example: Maybe 300 orders shipped last week

inputs_from_owner.label: The channels you control
inputs_from_owner.example: Website, Instagram, email list, Shopify order emails

inputs_from_owner.label: What has been said publicly so far, and by whom
inputs_from_owner.example: Nothing from us; two TikToks with 40k views

inputs_from_owner.label: Lawyer, insurer or regulator contacts
inputs_from_owner.example: Our attorney; our product-liability insurer

inputs_from_owner.label: Who speaks for the business
inputs_from_owner.example: Me, the owner

composition.why: Astrid runs the room. She writes the holding statement, chooses the response strategy (SCCT) and keeps one voice and an update rhythm.
Patricia sequences who hears what, from whom and when, so no one learns the news second-hand, and chairs the approval of the words.
Einar contains the operational problem and runs the fix plan with a RAID log and a steady status cadence.
Aroha handles the affected customers: HEARD-based replies, a remedy matrix and public review responses that calm rather than inflame.
Oona keeps a sourced timeline separating what's known, unknown and rumoured, so every word published is true.
Duc checks that fixes actually landed, then leads the blameless post-mortem once things are calm.
Gurpreet speaks for the regulator, the affected customer and the journalist. He names what the statement must never say and what could make things worse.

plan_skeleton.title: Sourced facts timeline
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A running timeline of what is known, unknown and rumoured, with a source for every fact and who is affected and how many; refreshed every hour until stable.
plan_skeleton.brief: Use SIFT and lateral reading on anything circulating publicly. Internal facts come from the owner and systems, with receipts.

plan_skeleton.title: Holding statement
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A holding statement under 120 words: what happened (facts only), who is affected, what we're doing and when we'll update; no speculation, blame or admission beyond the facts; channels and timing listed.
plan_skeleton.brief: Draft the first version within the hour. Empathy first, facts second, action third.

plan_skeleton.title: Licensed review before anything is published
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Where there is legal, privacy, safety or regulatory exposure, counsel has reviewed the statement and any notification duties are flagged with deadlines; the owner approves the exact text and channels before anything is published.
plan_skeleton.brief: If counsel can't be reached quickly, the owner decides whether to publish a shorter, facts-only version and records why.

plan_skeleton.title: Stakeholder communications plan
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A stakeholder map (affected customers, staff, suppliers, regulators, press and partners) with message, messenger, channel and timing; staff hear before the public, and affected customers before the press.
plan_skeleton.brief: Every message traces back to the approved holding statement; nobody improvises.

plan_skeleton.title: Containment and fix plan
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Containment actions with owners and times; a fix plan with a RAID log; what customers will see change, and when; status updates on a fixed cadence.
plan_skeleton.brief: Contain first, fix second, explain third. Every action the owner must approve is marked.

plan_skeleton.title: Customer remedies and responses
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A remedy matrix by customer impact; HEARD-based replies for email, DMs and public reviews; nothing promised that operations can't deliver; nothing sent before approval.
plan_skeleton.brief: Remedies match the approved statement and the fix plan. Replies are drafts the owner sends, following the workspace rule that customer-facing AI work is labelled.

plan_skeleton.title: Blameless post-mortem
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A blameless post-mortem covering the timeline, contributing factors (5 Whys), what went well, and changes with owners and dates, plus response-time metrics; the lessons are saved to memory.
plan_skeleton.brief: Focus on systems, not people. Every change has an owner and a date, or it isn't a change.

deliverables.name: Containment and fix plan with RAID log

meeting_moments.title: War-room kickoff: the first 15 minutes
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Astrid sets the rules: facts before words, one voice, updates on the hour. Oona says what's confirmed and what's rumour, Einar what's being contained, and Gurpreet what could make it worse. You can join and answer questions directly.

meeting_moments.title: Approve the words
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Patricia chairs. Astrid reads the statement aloud, Oona confirms every fact in it, and Gurpreet says what it must not say. You approve the exact words and channels, subject to counsel.

meeting_moments.title: Hourly stand-up
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Two minutes each hour: Einar on what's fixed, Aroha on what customers are saying, and Astrid on the next update. You can listen in from your phone.

meeting_moments.title: Post-mortem retro
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Duc leads a blameless retro covering what happened, why, what worked, and the changes with owners and dates. You hear it once, calmly, after the storm.

duration_estimate.note: Holding statement within the first hour: facts and drafts run on faster models, and only the statement review and licensed-review packet use the deep tier. Full cycle over about two days.

lines: This morning some customers received another customer's order confirmation.
We have stopped the email system, identified the cause and are contacting everyone affected.
No payment details were exposed. We will update you by 4 pm today.
Facts only; approved by you, with counsel consulted on notification duties.

model_hints.note: Speed first: drafting runs on fast or balanced models so the holding statement lands inside the hour; the deep tier is reserved for reviewing that statement and preparing the licensed-review packet.

success_criteria: Every fact in the statement appears on the timeline with a source.
A holding statement is ready for approval within the first hour, and nothing is published without the owner's approval and counsel's review where there is exposure.
Staff and affected customers hear before the public and the press.
Every containment action has an owner and a time, and updates go out on the promised cadence.
The post-mortem lists changes with owners and dates, and the lessons are saved to memory.

recipes.name: Strategy offsite in a box
recipes.outcome: Pre-work analysis, a facilitated agenda, strategic choices and an OKR draft.
recipes.when_to_use: You're taking a day or two with your leadership team (or just you and a co-founder) to decide where the business goes next, and you want it to end in real choices and goals rather than a whiteboard photo nobody looks at again.

inputs_from_owner.label: Who's attending, when, and whether it's in person or remote
inputs_from_owner.example: Me and 3 managers; one day in person on 14 November

inputs_from_owner.label: The big questions you want answered
inputs_from_owner.example: Should we open a second location or go online? What do we stop doing?

inputs_from_owner.label: Recent results and financials (or connect accounting)
inputs_from_owner.example: 2025 P&L and monthly revenue

inputs_from_owner.label: Your current strategy, plans or goals
inputs_from_owner.example: Last year's goals on one slide

inputs_from_owner.label: Customer feedback or reviews to consider
inputs_from_owner.example: Google reviews and our NPS comments

composition.why: Elijah designs and runs the offsite with Liberating Structures, timeboxes and a clear decision rule, so it ends in choices, not just conversation.
Adaeze brings the Five Forces and SWOT-to-TOWS pre-work and captures the choices as a Playing to Win cascade.
Callum tears down three to five competitors, covering offer, pricing, positioning and recent moves, with sources.
Ingrid turns the decisions into next quarter's OKRs before the energy fades.
Ruth steelmans the road not taken and pre-mortems every option, so the team decides with its eyes open.

plan_skeleton.title: Competitor teardown
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A teardown of three to five competitors (offer, pricing, positioning and recent moves) with sources; the industry forces that most shape profit next year named.
plan_skeleton.brief: Public information only, cited, with the date of each observation.

plan_skeleton.title: Five Forces, SWOT and TOWS options
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A Five Forces summary and a SWOT built from evidence rather than opinion, converted into TOWS strategic options; the three biggest strategic questions for the offsite stated.
plan_skeleton.brief: Every SWOT item cites evidence from the results, the reviews or the teardown.

plan_skeleton.title: Pre-read and facilitated agenda
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A pre-read under six pages framing the questions, evidence and options; a timeboxed agenda with a Liberating Structure for each segment (1-2-4-All, TRIZ, 15% Solutions) and a stated decision rule; the pre-read goes to attendees only on the owner's approval.
plan_skeleton.brief: Build in energy breaks and a parking lot. The decision rule is agreed before the day, not on it.

plan_skeleton.title: Steelman and pre-mortem the options
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES. Each strategic option is steelmanned and pre-mortemed; the choice the team is avoiding is named.
plan_skeleton.brief: Speak for customers, competitors and the version of the team a year from now.

plan_skeleton.title: The offsite session
plan_skeleton.acceptance: The session runs with the owner and team; where-to-play and how-to-win choices are recorded with the decision rule used; a stop-doing list is agreed; the minutes list owners and dates.
plan_skeleton.brief: Elijah facilitates live, Adaeze captures the cascade, and Ruth gets one timeboxed challenge per choice.

plan_skeleton.title: Strategy one-pager
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A Playing to Win cascade on one page that reflects the offsite decisions word for word; trade-offs are explicit, and nothing appears that wasn't decided.
plan_skeleton.brief: If something important wasn't decided, list it as an open question rather than filling the gap.

plan_skeleton.title: Next-quarter OKR draft
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Next-quarter OKRs (at most three objectives with two to four key results each) traced to the strategic choices, with owners, baselines and a weekly check-in cadence.
plan_skeleton.brief: Draft with the owners' names from the minutes; confirm confidence scores with each of them.

deliverables.name: Five Forces, SWOT and TOWS options

meeting_moments.title: What keeps you up at night?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Elijah asks what a successful offsite would change on Monday, Adaeze asks which decision you've been putting off, and Callum asks which competitor you watch most closely. Twenty minutes that shape the whole agenda.

meeting_moments.title: The road not taken
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Ruth steelmans the option everyone is quietly dismissing, Adaeze defends the favourite, Callum brings what competitors are actually doing, and Elijah keeps it to the evidence. You arrive at the offsite with the hard questions already asked.

meeting_moments.title: The offsite
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Elijah facilitates your session live: 1-2-4-All on the big questions, TRIZ on what to stop, and a consent decision on each choice. Adaeze captures the cascade and Ingrid drafts goals as you decide.

meeting_moments.title: The strategy in two minutes
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Adaeze reads the one-page strategy you chose and Ingrid reads next quarter's objectives. Play it to your team on Monday.

Decisions will be recorded with owners and the first-quarter OKRs.

Every major option was steelmanned and pre-mortemed before the offsite.

recipes.name: Software or vendor selection
recipes.outcome: Requirements, a shortlist, a weighted comparison and a recommendation with negotiation notes.
recipes.when_to_use: You need to choose a new tool, system or supplier (a CRM, POS, payroll, 3PL or accounting system) and every demo looks the same. You want a fair comparison against your real needs, the true cost over three years, and a negotiating position before you sign.

inputs_from_owner.label: What you're buying and the problem it must solve
inputs_from_owner.example: A CRM to replace spreadsheets for 6 salespeople

inputs_from_owner.label: Who will use it and at what volume
inputs_from_owner.example: 6 in sales, 2 in ops; about 400 deals a year

inputs_from_owner.label: Budget, and when you need it live
inputs_from_owner.example: Under $15k a year; live by February

inputs_from_owner.label: Your current tool and its contract end date
inputs_from_owner.example: Pipedrive, renews 31 January

inputs_from_owner.label: Must-have integrations
inputs_from_owner.example: Gmail, QuickBooks, website forms

inputs_from_owner.label: Vendors already on your radar
inputs_from_owner.example: HubSpot, Salesforce Starter

composition.why: Viktor runs a fair process: the shortlist, the RFQ, a weighted comparison and three-year total cost of ownership.
Precious turns how you work into testable requirements and spots overlaps with tools you already pay for.
Martina checks each finalist's security posture, DPA, sub-processors and data-export terms.
Idris builds the negotiation plan (runner-up as BATNA, price caps, exit terms, timing) and chairs the winner-versus-runner-up debate.
Jelena speaks for future you, trying to leave. She tests integration fit, data portability, exit cost and the build-versus-buy alternative.
Eleanor reads the MSA and DPA schedules first, lists the terms that matter (liability caps, auto-renewal, exit and data return) and prepares the licensed-review packet.

plan_skeleton.title: Requirements and current-stack overlap
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Current tools and spend in this category, overlaps to retire, and requirements split into must, should and could, covering users, integrations, data and budget; every must-have can be tested in a demo.
plan_skeleton.brief: Write requirements as scenarios ('a salesperson logs a call from their phone in under 30 seconds'), not feature names.

plan_skeleton.title: Market scan and shortlist
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A long list of 8–12 vendors from independent sources, filtered to three or four on the must-haves with reasons; RFQ or RFI questions drafted; nothing is sent to vendors without approval.
plan_skeleton.brief: Independent reviews and documentation over vendor marketing; note any reviewer conflicts of interest.

plan_skeleton.title: Security and contract-terms review
plan_skeleton.acceptance: For each shortlisted vendor: public security posture (SOC 2 or ISO report availability, SSO and MFA, data location), DPA and sub-processors, exit and data-export terms; red flags ranked.
plan_skeleton.brief: Use each vendor's trust center and published terms. Ask for reports under NDA only with the owner's approval.

plan_skeleton.title: Weighted comparison and 3-year TCO
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A weighted scoring matrix agreed with the owner before scoring; three-year total cost of ownership (licences, implementation, training and switching); a sensitivity check showing whether the winner changes under different weights.
plan_skeleton.brief: Score from demo evidence and documentation, never from the sales pitch alone.

plan_skeleton.title: Lock-in and build-versus-buy challenge
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES. Integration fit, data portability, exit cost and the build-versus-buy alternative are assessed, and the recommendation is recorded as an ADR with consequences.
plan_skeleton.brief: Ask how the data gets out, in what format, and what breaks when it does.

plan_skeleton.title: Negotiation notes per finalist
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A negotiation plan for each finalist: the BATNA (the runner-up), target price and terms (term length, price caps, SLAs, exit) and a concession sequence timed around the vendor's quarter-end.
plan_skeleton.brief: Nothing is agreed with a vendor by the team; the owner negotiates or approves every message.

plan_skeleton.title: Licensed review of contract terms before signing
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Counsel (and a privacy professional where personal data flows) has reviewed the chosen vendor's MSA and DPA issues; the owner approves the recommendation; nothing is signed before this.
plan_skeleton.brief: Eleanor packages the MSA and DPA issue list with Martina's security findings for an attorney, a privacy professional and, for high-risk access, a qualified security professional; each decision is recorded before anything is signed.

deliverables.name: RFQ and RFI drafts for the shortlist

meeting_moments.title: What must this tool do?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Precious asks how the work happens today and what the current tool gets wrong, Viktor asks about budget and timing, and Jelena asks what you'd need to take with you if you ever left. Your answers become testable requirements.

meeting_moments.title: Winner versus runner-up
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Idris chairs. Viktor argues for the top-scoring vendor, Jelena for whichever is easier to leave, and Martina raises the security and data terms. You hear the real trade-off, not the sales pitch.

meeting_moments.title: Choose and negotiate
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: A five-minute decision: Viktor's recommendation, Jelena's risks and Idris's opening position. You choose, and nothing is signed until counsel has reviewed the terms.

duration_estimate.note: Vendor demos and counsel review run on your calendar.

lines: Vendor A scores 82 (3-year TCO 14.2k); Vendor B 76 (11.9k); Vendor C fails a must-have (no data export).
A wins on integrations and support; B is cheaper but locks data behind a paid add-on.
Contract issues for your attorney: 36-month auto-renewal and an uncapped price increase.
Recommendation: A, with a negotiated 12-month term and an exit clause.

success_criteria: The scoring weights were agreed with the owner before any vendor was scored.
Three-year total cost of ownership includes implementation, training and switching costs.
Every finalist has a security and data-terms review, with red flags ranked.
The recommendation is recorded as an ADR with consequences and an exit path.
Nothing is signed before counsel has reviewed it and the owner has approved it.

variants_by_industry.changes: Selecting POS, reservations and scheduling tools with menu, labor and payments integration.
Practice-management or scheduling software: BAAs, audit logs and minimum-necessary access.
Project-management and estimating software, with field usability tests.
Practice management, billing and trust-accounting fit.
Choosing a 3PL or fulfillment partner, with SLAs, cut-offs and rate cards.
ERP or MRP selection, with BOM and routing fit.

recipes.name: Weekly operating rhythm
recipes.outcome: A scorecard, weekly review ritual, meeting cadence and daily brief that run on their own.
recipes.when_to_use: Every week feels like firefighting: meetings run long, numbers arrive late, and things slip because nobody owned them. You want a simple rhythm (one scorecard, one weekly review, a short daily brief) that runs itself.

inputs_from_owner.label: Your current meetings and calendar (or connect your calendar)
inputs_from_owner.example: Monday team meeting (90 minutes, no agenda); ad-hoc check-ins

inputs_from_owner.label: The numbers you check today, and where
inputs_from_owner.example: Sales in Square, bookings in Calendly, cash in the bank app

inputs_from_owner.label: Team members and what they own
inputs_from_owner.example: Maya runs ops, Tomi sales, Priya bookkeeping

inputs_from_owner.label: Current goals or OKRs
inputs_from_owner.example: Hit $80k a month; cut no-shows below 5%

inputs_from_owner.label: When and where you want the daily brief
inputs_from_owner.example: 7:30am on Slack, with audio

composition.why: Yolanda designs the operating cadence and the EOS-style scorecard, and makes sure every number and every issue has an owner.
Ingrid designs the weekly review, facilitates the 'design your week' workshop and ties the scorecard to your goals.
Winston produces the daily brief and the weekly review pack, and captures decisions and actions with owners and dates.
Hugo builds the scorecard so it fills itself from your connectors and computes red and green, so nobody types them.
Dawit speaks for week six, when nobody opens the scorecard. He pre-mortems the rhythm and builds in the countermeasures.

plan_skeleton.title: Scorecard numbers and owners
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Five to fifteen weekly numbers, each with an owner, a target and a red/green rule; every number comes from a connector or a two-minute manual entry.
plan_skeleton.brief: Choose leading indicators the team can influence this week, not only lagging results.

plan_skeleton.title: Scorecard build
plan_skeleton.acceptance: The scorecard fills itself from connectors where possible, shows a 13-week trend and has an entry form for manual numbers; red and green are computed, never typed.
plan_skeleton.brief: Readable on a phone, because that is where most owners will check it.

plan_skeleton.title: Meeting cadence and weekly review agenda
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A cadence map (daily huddle, weekly review, monthly and quarterly) with purpose, attendees, length and inputs; a weekly review agenda under 90 minutes covering the scorecard, goals and an issues list solved one issue at a time; the meetings to cut are listed.
plan_skeleton.brief: Every meeting has a purpose it alone serves, or it is cut or merged.

plan_skeleton.title: Daily brief setup
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A daily brief (text plus a 90-second audio version) assembled from the scorecard, calendar and open issues; the owner approves the delivery time and channel; the first three briefs are checked for noise. Activation runs under an owner-approved standing grant (automation id, audience, trigger, rate and spend caps, expiry within 90 days, kill switch, receipt log); every run writes a receipt.
plan_skeleton.brief: Lead with what needs the owner today; everything else goes below the fold.

plan_skeleton.title: Weekly review pack and minutes
plan_skeleton.acceptance: The weekly review pack is generated before each meeting; minutes and actions (with owner and date) are captured afterwards; unresolved issues roll forward; nothing is scheduled without owner approval. Activation runs under an owner-approved standing grant (automation id, audience, trigger, rate and spend caps, expiry within 90 days, kill switch, receipt log); every run writes a receipt.
plan_skeleton.brief: Actions without an owner and a date are sent back to the meeting, not recorded.

plan_skeleton.title: Adoption pre-mortem
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES. The premise: it's week six and nobody opens the scorecard. Why? Each failure mode (stale numbers, meeting creep, no owner) has a countermeasure built in, and a four-week trial with a retro date is set.
plan_skeleton.brief: Assume the rhythm will decay and design for the laziest good week.

deliverables.name: Weekly review agenda and issues list
Daily brief
deliverables.description: A 90-second voiced brief, delivered at the time the owner approved.

meeting_moments.title: How does your week actually run?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Yolanda asks what you look at on Monday morning and what surprises you on Friday, Ingrid asks which meetings you'd happily cancel, and Winston asks how you like to be briefed. Fifteen minutes.

meeting_moments.title: Design your week
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Ingrid facilitates while you and the team pick the scorecard numbers, set the red/green rules and agree the weekly review agenda. Dawit keeps asking 'who owns this?' until every number has a name next to it.

meeting_moments.title: Your first daily brief
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Winston reads tomorrow's brief exactly as you'll hear it at 7:30: yesterday's numbers, today's calendar, what's red and what needs you. Tell him what to cut.

meeting_moments.title: Four-week retro
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: After the trial, Dawit leads a short retro on which numbers went stale, which meetings ran over and what nobody read. The rhythm gets simpler, not bigger.

duration_estimate.note: One week to set up, followed by a four-week trial and a retro.

lines: 11 numbers, each with an owner and a red/green rule; 8 fill themselves from connectors.
Red this week: quote win rate 22% (target 30%) and 3 jobs over budget.
Weekly review agenda: 15 minutes on the scorecard, then the top 3 issues only.
Daily brief at 7:30 am, 90 seconds, running under your approved standing grant.

success_criteria: Every scorecard number has an owner, a target and a computed red/green rule.
The weekly review fits its timebox and ends with actions that each have an owner and a date.
The daily brief arrives at the approved time for four weeks, with fewer than one noise complaint a week.
Total weekly meeting time falls, or stays flat while decisions get faster.
The four-week retro takes place and simplifies at least one element of the rhythm.

variants_by_industry.changes: A weekly job-site huddle covering schedule, safety and change-order status, with a toolbox talk every Monday.
A daily pre-shift and a weekly P&L, with prime cost, covers and reviews on the scorecard.
Utilization, pipeline and delivery health on the scorecard, plus a weekly resourcing huddle.
A weekly metrics review with MRR, activation and incidents, plus a monthly board-style summary.
A daily huddle on schedule fill, no-shows and front-desk issues (non-clinical).
Store huddles, a weekly sell-through review and staffing to traffic.

recipes.name: Restaurant profit tune-up
recipes.outcome: Menu engineering, prime-cost targets, a labor schedule and a guest-recovery script.
recipes.when_to_use: Sales are fine, but there isn't enough left at the end of the month. Food costs creep up, labor runs over on slow nights, some dishes sell well but earn little, and one bad night online costs you regulars. You want a focused tune-up of the levers that move restaurant profit.

inputs_from_owner.label: 8–12 weeks of item-level sales from your POS (or connect it)
inputs_from_owner.example: Toast item sales export

inputs_from_owner.label: Recipes or specs, plus recent supplier invoices
inputs_from_owner.example: Photos of the recipe binder; Sysco invoices

inputs_from_owner.label: Labor reports or schedules, and pay rates
inputs_from_owner.example: 7shifts schedules; Gusto payroll summary

inputs_from_owner.label: Your current menu (file or photo)
inputs_from_owner.example: Dinner menu PDF

inputs_from_owner.label: Your location(s) and jurisdiction
inputs_from_owner.example: One location, Chicago IL

inputs_from_owner.label: Recent reviews or guest complaints
inputs_from_owner.example: Google and Yelp reviews from the last 3 months

composition.why: Nabil runs Kasavana-Smith menu engineering and sets prime-cost targets the way a seasoned GM would, one plate and one shift at a time.
Tendai costs every plate with real yields and invoice prices, and builds the labor-to-sales schedule.
Aroha writes the guest-recovery script, the comp matrix and review responses that turn a bad night into a regular.
Zofia redesigns the menu so the stars sit where eyes land, then delivers it print-ready.
Omar speaks for your regulars and the place down the street. He challenges every price move and insists on a staged test with a stop rule.
Beverly checks the schedule against overtime, break, tip-pool and predictive-scheduling rules and prepares the packet for employment counsel, so labor savings never turn into a wage claim.

plan_skeleton.title: Recipe costing and plate margins
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A yield-adjusted plate cost for every menu item from recipes and current supplier prices; food-cost % and contribution margin per item; missing recipes listed rather than guessed.
plan_skeleton.brief: Use as-purchased prices and real yields (trim, cooking loss), not the price per pound on the invoice alone.

plan_skeleton.title: Menu engineering matrix
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A Kasavana-Smith matrix (stars, plowhorses, puzzles and dogs) from POS mix and contribution margin; for each item, a keep, reprice, re-plate, reposition or remove call with the expected margin impact.
plan_skeleton.brief: Consider the guest experience too: a 'dog' that anchors a regular's visit might stay.

plan_skeleton.title: Price and mix challenge
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES. Each proposed price change is checked against local competitor prices and its likely effect on covers; a staged test (one daypart or item group first) with a stop rule.
plan_skeleton.brief: Small, frequent price moves on stars beat one big menu-wide increase.

plan_skeleton.title: Prime-cost targets and leak list
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A weekly prime-cost target (COGS plus total labor) against the current baseline, by daypart; the five biggest leaks (waste, comps, overtime, over-portioning, voids) sized in dollars.
plan_skeleton.brief: Prime cost is reviewed weekly, not monthly. The leak list names who can fix each leak.

plan_skeleton.title: Labor-to-sales schedule template
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A labor-to-sales schedule template by forecast covers and daypart, with minimum staffing for safety and service; break, overtime, tip and scheduling-notice rules flagged by jurisdiction; only the owner publishes it.
plan_skeleton.brief: Staff to the forecast rather than habit, and never below the safe minimum for the floor and the line.

plan_skeleton.title: Licensed review of labor schedule rules
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Employment counsel or a qualified HR professional has confirmed the break, overtime, tip and predictive-scheduling rules for the location; changes are applied before the schedule is published.
plan_skeleton.brief: Beverly packages the tip-pool, overtime, break and predictive-scheduling questions with the proposed schedule for employment counsel or a qualified HR professional, and records each decision.

plan_skeleton.title: Menu redesign, print-ready
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A menu layout that applies the matrix (stars in prime positions, no price columns, clear descriptions) as a print-ready PDF with specs; allergen and dietary labels carried over unchanged from the owner's data.
plan_skeleton.brief: Never write or change allergen information; take it verbatim from the kitchen's own records.

plan_skeleton.title: Guest-recovery script and review responses
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A HEARD-based guest-recovery script for floor staff, a comp and remedy matrix with dollar limits by role, and three review-response templates in the house voice; nothing is posted without approval.
plan_skeleton.brief: Recovery at the table beats recovery online, so the script is written to be used mid-service.

meeting_moments.title: Walk us through a Friday night
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Nabil asks where the night goes sideways (the rush, the 86s, the comps), Tendai asks how you price a new dish, and Aroha asks what happened the last time a table left unhappy. It sounds like a chat with a seasoned GM, and in a sense it is one.

meeting_moments.title: Raise, re-plate or remove?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Omar challenges each price move against the place down the street and your regulars, Nabil defends the plate, and Zofia shows where each dish should sit on the menu. You hear the plan item by item.

meeting_moments.title: Guest-recovery role-play
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Nabil plays an upset guest whose steak came out wrong on a full Saturday, and Aroha shows the HEARD recovery step by step. Play it at your next pre-shift.

duration_estimate.note: Price changes then run as a staged test over two to four weeks.

lines: Stars: lamb shoulder and the burger; keep them in the top-right of the menu.
Plowhorse: fish and chips (high sales, 58% food cost); re-cost the portion or reprice by 1.50.
Dog: the quinoa bowl (6 sold a week); retire it or rework it.
Prime cost 67% last month against a 62% target; labor at Tuesday lunch is the biggest leak.

success_criteria: Every menu item has a yield-adjusted plate cost and a contribution margin.
Every item on the matrix has a keep, reprice, re-plate, reposition or remove call with its expected margin impact.
A weekly prime-cost target exists, and the top five leaks are sized in dollars.
The labor template meets minimum staffing and was checked by counsel or an HR professional before publishing.
Floor staff have a guest-recovery script with remedy limits by role.

duration_estimate.note: Most of the calendar time is the survey window; drafts are ready in the first hour.

lines: Response rate 81% (13 of 16); results shown only for groups of five or more.
Strongest link to intent to stay: 'I know what's expected of me', which scores 3.1 of 5.
Second: schedule predictability; weekend closes fall on the same three people.
Pay ranks fifth; two roles sit below market (pay check attached for your review).
Three actions: scorecards for every role, a fair close rotation, and monthly 1:1s.

success_criteria: Results are shown only for groups at or above the anonymity threshold.
Actions target the top two or three drivers, each with an owner and a date.
Stay interviews are voluntary and use the same core questions for everyone.
Pay-equity and role-change questions go to counsel before anything is announced.
A re-pulse date is set to measure change.

variants_by_industry.changes: Mobile-first survey for shift staff, rota fairness and tip transparency as likely drivers.
Front-desk burnout and schedule load; nothing clinical is surveyed.
Field crews: van time, weekend on-call rotation and safety concerns are asked about directly.
Store and warehouse teams: shift fairness and peak-season load.
Mission fatigue and volunteer-versus-staff load; stay interviews include volunteers who lead.

recipes.name: AI adoption plan
recipes.outcome: An inventory of AI tools in use with risk tiers, a data traffic-light policy, three high-return use cases with golden-set evals and approval gates, and the integrations they need.
recipes.when_to_use: Your team already uses AI tools (officially or not), you want the benefits without leaking data or getting tricked, and you'd like three use cases that actually pay off.

inputs_from_owner.label: AI tools you know the team uses
inputs_from_owner.example: Chat assistants, a transcription app, an AI feature in our CRM

inputs_from_owner.label: The kinds of data your business handles
inputs_from_owner.example: Customer contact details, invoices, some health notes

inputs_from_owner.label: Where the team loses the most time
inputs_from_owner.example: Answering the same booking emails; copying invoice data

inputs_from_owner.label: Main systems (email, CRM, accounting, helpdesk)
inputs_from_owner.example: Google Workspace, HubSpot, Xero

composition.why: Avery inventories what's already in use, sets the data traffic light and designs approvals people will actually follow.
Aditi builds a golden set for each use case and won't call anything ready until it passes.
Ibrahim plans the connections each use case needs, with least-privilege access and nothing that runs twice.
Felipe times the manual work and shortlists the use cases worth doing first.
Sebastián maps where personal data would flow and keeps it out of tools you have not approved.
Walter asks of every use case: would a spreadsheet formula or a simple rule do this cheaper and more reliably?

plan_skeleton.title: AI tool inventory and risk tiers
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Every AI tool in use (approved or not) with owner, purpose, data classes, vendor terms and a risk tier.

plan_skeleton.title: Data traffic-light and acceptable-use policy
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A two-page policy: green, amber and red data, what never goes into AI tools, disclosure rules, and how to request a new tool.

plan_skeleton.title: Three high-return use cases
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Three use cases scored on hours saved, risk tier and data class, each surviving the question "would a formula or rule do?".

plan_skeleton.title: Golden sets and pass thresholds
plan_skeleton.acceptance: At least 30 real, de-identified cases per use case, with pass thresholds and zero-tolerance failures set before any tuning.

plan_skeleton.title: Integration plan
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Connections, scopes, data flows and failure handling for each use case, with least-privilege access.

plan_skeleton.title: Approval gates and standing grants
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Every AI action that sends, publishes, pays or changes data has a human approval or an owner-approved standing grant with caps, expiry and a kill switch.

plan_skeleton.title: Licensed review of the AI policy and data flows
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A privacy professional or counsel has reviewed the policy and data flows, and a qualified security professional any high-risk access, before rollout.
plan_skeleton.brief: Sebastián packages the data map; Avery the policy and gates.

deliverables.name: AI tool inventory with risk tiers

Three use cases with eval results

meeting_moments.title: What are people already using?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Avery asks which tools are in use (no blame), Felipe asks where the hours go, and Aditi asks what 'right' looks like for each task.

meeting_moments.title: AI, or just a formula?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Walter argues for the simplest tool; Felipe and Aditi make the case for AI where it earns it. Three use cases survive, and you hear why.

meeting_moments.title: What you are approving
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: The policy on one page, the three use cases with their test results, and the approvals each will need.

example_output.deliverable: AI tool inventory and use cases
lines: 14 AI tools found in use; 5 not approved (browser extensions and a free transcription app).
Red data (customer health notes) is being pasted into one unapproved tool: stop now; an approved alternative is proposed.
Use case 1: draft replies to routine booking emails, about 4 hours a week, amber data, human approves each send.
Use case 2: invoice data capture, about 3 hours a week; a spreadsheet rule handles 60% of it before any AI.

success_criteria: Every AI tool in use is inventoried with an owner, data class and risk tier.
The data traffic-light policy fits on two pages and names what never goes into AI tools.
Each use case has a golden set and a pass threshold set before tuning.
Every AI action with an external effect has an approval gate or a standing grant.
The policy and data flows pass licensed review before rollout.

variants_by_industry.changes: Protected health information stays out of AI tools unless the vendor and agreement are approved; front-desk use cases only.
Privilege and client confidentiality rules; no client data in consumer tools; attorney approves every use case.
Client data separation per engagement and disclosure of AI use in deliverables.
Product content, support replies and returns triage as candidate use cases.
Student data rules and parents' consent where minors are involved.

recipes.name: Margin rescue
recipes.outcome: A price-volume-mix bridge, cost-to-serve by customer, a supplier and software spend audit, a payment-fee review, price-increase candidates and a 90-day savings plan.
recipes.when_to_use: Your margins are sliding, you're busier than ever but keeping less, and you want to know exactly where the money is going before cutting anything.

inputs_from_owner.label: P&L for this year and last, and sales by product or customer
inputs_from_owner.example: Xero P&L and Shopify sales by product

inputs_from_owner.label: The margin you want back to
inputs_from_owner.example: Gross margin back above 40%

inputs_from_owner.label: Main suppliers and software subscriptions
inputs_from_owner.example: Card statements show most subscriptions

inputs_from_owner.label: Payment processor statements
inputs_from_owner.example: Stripe and Square fee reports

composition.why: Tendai splits the margin change into price, volume, mix and cost, then finds which customers and products cost more than they earn.
Viktor audits supplier spend and payment fees and re-quotes what should be cheaper.
Omar finds price-increase candidates and designs them as tests with a stop rule, not blanket rises.
Precious finds the software subscriptions nobody uses and who owns the rest.
Harriet challenges every saving that looks good on paper but hurts cash, customers or next quarter.

plan_skeleton.title: Price-volume-mix bridge
plan_skeleton.acceptance: The margin change split into price, volume, mix and cost effects that sum exactly to the total.

plan_skeleton.title: Cost to serve by customer
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Margin after cost to serve (delivery, support, rush orders, returns, payment terms) by customer or segment.

plan_skeleton.title: Supplier spend audit
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Top suppliers by spend with price trend, alternatives and a re-quote plan for the top three.

plan_skeleton.title: Software spend audit
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Every subscription with owner, usage and renewal date; unused and duplicate tools listed for cancellation approval.

plan_skeleton.title: Payment-fee review
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Effective processing rate by processor and card type, with pricing options (for example interchange-plus) compared.

plan_skeleton.title: Price-increase candidates and tests
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Candidate products or customers for a price move, each as a staged test with a stop rule.

plan_skeleton.title: 90-day savings plan
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Every saving with an owner, a date, the evidence behind it and the total reconciled to the P&L.

meeting_moments.title: Where did the margin go?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Tendai asks what changed in what you sell and to whom; Viktor asks about suppliers and fees; Harriet asks how much cash room you have.

meeting_moments.title: Raise prices, or cut costs first?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Omar makes the case for targeted price tests; Harriet asks what each does to cash and customers. You hear the trade-off before anything changes.

meeting_moments.title: Your 90-day plan
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: The savings that are safe to start now, the ones that need testing, and what they add up to against your target.

lines: Gross margin fell from 41.2% to 36.8%: price +0.6 pts, mix -2.9 pts (more wholesale), cost -2.1 pts (freight).
Three customers cost more to serve than they earn: two small wholesale accounts and one with weekly rush orders.
Software: 9 of 31 subscriptions unused (4,860 a year); an interchange-plus quote would save about 0.4 pts on card fees.
90-day plan: a wholesale minimum order, a freight re-quote, cancel 9 tools, and test a 6% increase on 3 product lines.

success_criteria: The margin bridge sums exactly to the total change.
Cost to serve is shown per customer or segment with its drivers.
Every saving has an owner, a date and its evidence.
Price moves are staged tests with a stop rule, not blanket increases.
The plan's total is reconciled to the P&L.

variants_by_industry.changes: Menu engineering and prime cost replace product mix; supplier re-quotes focus on the top 20 ingredients.
Scrap, changeover time and OEE join the bridge as cost drivers.
Utilization, realization and scope creep by client replace product mix.
Shipping, returns and marketplace fees by product; free-shipping threshold tested.
Job costing by job type with drive time and callbacks; price book tiers tested on new quotes first.
Hosting cost per customer, discounting and payment failures join the bridge.

recipes.name: Client intake streamline
recipes.outcome: Faster, calmer client intake: a short intake form, a conflict-check or eligibility step, scheduling and reminders, and a front-desk SOP, reviewed before launch.
recipes.when_to_use: Enquiries wait too long for a reply, consults no-show, or intake is a tangle of emails and phone tag, in a law firm, a coaching or education business, or another professional practice.

inputs_from_owner.label: How a new client reaches you today and what happens next
inputs_from_owner.example: Web form, then an email thread, then a phone consult

inputs_from_owner.label: What you must know before a first meeting
inputs_from_owner.example: Other parties involved, deadlines, budget

inputs_from_owner.label: Practice or booking tools you use
inputs_from_owner.example: Clio and Calendly

inputs_from_owner.label: Enquiries per week and no-show rate, if known
inputs_from_owner.example: About 25 a week; maybe 1 in 4 no-shows

composition.why: Daniel maps intake end to end, builds the conflict-check step and makes sure every legal judgement stays with your attorneys.
Felipe builds the scheduling and reminder flows in test mode, with a kill switch.
Aoife rewrites the intake form so it asks only what you need, in plain language, on a phone.
Sebastián keeps intake data to the minimum and checks consent for texts and recordings.
Dilani speaks for the stressed first-time client: she tests the intake with five people before you launch.

plan_skeleton.title: Current intake map and baseline
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Channels, time to first reply, drop-off points, the conflict-check step and the no-show rate, mapped from real enquiries.

plan_skeleton.title: Short, plain intake form
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Asks only what intake needs, in plain language, works on a phone, and gives no legal advice in any field.

plan_skeleton.title: Conflict-check or eligibility step
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A defined step that runs before scheduling, with who decides; every conflict or eligibility decision is made by the attorney or owner.

plan_skeleton.title: Scheduling and reminder flows
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Consult booked in the same session; reminders at 48 hours and 2 hours with confirm or reschedule; texts only with documented consent. Built in test mode first. Runs only under an owner-approved standing grant (automation id, audience, trigger, rate and spend caps, expiry within 90 days, kill switch, receipt log).

plan_skeleton.title: Five-person intake walkthrough
plan_skeleton.acceptance: First line APPROVED or CHANGES: five people complete the intake; the top friction points are fixed or listed.

plan_skeleton.title: Front-desk intake SOP
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Who does what from first contact to booked consult, with scripts that route any legal question to an attorney.

plan_skeleton.title: Licensed review of intake terms, conflicts process and privacy notice
plan_skeleton.acceptance: An attorney has reviewed the intake terms and conflicts process, and a privacy professional or counsel the privacy notice and consent language, before launch.
plan_skeleton.brief: Daniel packages the flow, the form and the SOP for review.

meeting_moments.title: How does a client find you today?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Daniel walks the intake from first message to consult, Dilani asks where clients get stuck, and Felipe asks what is done by hand.

meeting_moments.title: Would a stressed first-time client finish this?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Dilani plays back what five people did; Aoife fixes the words and Felipe the flow; Sebastián checks nothing collects more than it should.

meeting_moments.title: Ready to launch?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: The new flow, the reminder schedule, and what is waiting on your attorney before it goes live.

lines: Today: 38% of web enquiries wait more than 24 hours for a reply; about 1 in 4 consults no-show.
New flow: 9 intake questions (down from 23), a conflict check before scheduling, and the consult booked in the same session.
Reminders at 48 and 2 hours with confirm or reschedule; texts only with consent.
Your attorney approves every conflict decision and the engagement letter template.

success_criteria: The intake form collects only what intake needs, in plain language.
Every conflict or eligibility decision is made by the attorney or owner, never by coworkers.
Reminders run only under a standing grant, with SMS consent.
Five people complete the intake in the walkthrough and the top friction is fixed.
Intake terms, the conflicts process and the privacy notice pass licensed review before launch.

variants_by_industry.changes: Conflicts rules, trust-account deposits and engagement letters by jurisdiction; nothing in intake is legal advice.
Eligibility and fit replace conflicts (level, goals, schedule); the client agreement, refund terms and privacy notice still get licensed review.
Scope and fit screening replace conflicts; the engagement terms and privacy notice get licensed review.
